events.text: A black robe you have never seen before is sitting on your step when you come out. "The Hall Below the Throne takes its new year at the first frost," she says. "Four years. Those who go up the Ninth Stair come out somebody. Those who do not go at all stay whatever they were." She does not stand up. She is prepared to wait.

choices.text: Say you will be there at the first frost

effects.log: She nods and puts a small black tally stick in your hand. There is nothing written on it yet.

choices.text: Say you will make your own way up

effects.log: She looks at you for a moment, then writes something down. "That also goes in the tally," she says, and leaves.

events.text: The letter has no greeting. It lists, in a small tidy hand, every fight you have had since you were twelve, who won, and why. At the bottom: "The Hall Below the Throne has an empty cell. You are expected to think this is an honour. It is." Someone has been keeping count of you for years.

choices.text: Go and meet whoever keeps these lists

effects.log: You pack that night. If somebody is going to count you, you want to read the book.

choices.text: Burn it, and fight better

effects.log: You burn the letter. It occurs to you, watching it, that a copy surely exists.

events.text: The elders of {sda_house} have come to see you, three of them, in their good robes. All the Demon's children go down to the Hall sooner or later, they say, and the other houses have already sent theirs. "Whoever you meet on that stair," the eldest tells you, "you will meet again across a table, with knives under it. Better you learn their faces at fifteen."

choices.text: Tell them you will go, and bring back faces

effects.log: They bow, a little lower than they did when they came in. You are already worth more to them.

choices.text: Tell them you will not be raced against your brothers

effects.log: Nobody argues. The eldest simply looks tired, and your house feels colder for a long while after.

events.text: A cell of four, cut out of the mountain: four mats, one lamp, one good blanket. Nobody has told you whose the blanket is, and you understand, slowly, that this is the first lesson. {npc} has already sat down on it and is looking at you. {gn_room} are looking at you as well. Up at the turn of the stair, a Tally Master is pretending to read.

choices.text: Take the blanket from {npc}

effects.log: You cross the cell. {npc} stands up, smiling for the first time. The Tally Master turns a page.

choices.text: Bow to {npc}, and take the mat beside {him}

effects.log: You sit down at {his} right hand. There are worse places to learn from. {npc} tosses you a corner of the blanket, to see if you will take it.

choices.text: Lie down by the door and say nothing

effects.log: You lie down by the door, cold, and keep your eyes open. By morning you know who talks in their sleep.

events.text: At the first meal the Hall sets out three bowls for four people, and walks away. {npc} takes a bowl without hurrying and looks round to see who else understands. {gn_room} have not moved. It is clear this will happen every day for four years, and that whatever is decided tonight is what will be remembered.

choices.text: Take {his} bowl out of {his} hands

effects.log: You take it. {npc} looks at {his} empty hands, and laughs, and hits you. The fight lasts until the lamp goes out.

choices.text: Take the second bowl, and hand it to {npc}

effects.log: You give it to {him} to give out. {npc} is quick. {He} looks at you with new interest and hands it back.

choices.text: Go hungry tonight and watch

effects.log: You go hungry. It teaches you more than the bowl would have. Hungry people are honest about each other.

events.text: "Whose name goes first on the cell door?" says the chalk-boy, bored, stick in hand. It seems to be a real question. The first name draws the cell's duties and its rations both, and takes its punishments too. {npc} says {his} own at once. {gn_room} say nothing. The chalk-boy looks at you, in no hurry at all.

choices.text: Say your own name, louder

effects.log: The chalk-boy shrugs: "Then settle it." The chalk waits on the ledge while you and {npc} settle it.

choices.text: Say {npc}'s name for {him}

effects.log: You say it. {npc} is surprised, and then not. You have just bought something, and you will find out what it cost later.

choices.text: Say that the chalk can write what it likes

effects.log: The chalk-boy nearly smiles. Four names go on the door in a circle, which nobody has done before, and it causes no end of trouble.

events.text: By your second winter the Hall has become a matter of tables. {gn_clique} would have you. It is the kind of table where people think like you, and they have told you so in a way that lets them deny it. The strongest table is the one everyone else watches. And nobody at all is sitting alone, except those who have chosen to and can afford it.

choices.text: Sit down at {gn_clique}

effects.log: Someone moves over without looking up. You are fed, and informed on, and defended. It is more than you expected.

choices.text: Go to the strongest table and stand there until they make room

effects.log: It takes eleven days. On the twelfth, somebody moves their elbow. You have never been so proud of an elbow.

choices.text: Bring your cell to a table of your own

effects.log: You drag the bench out yourself. Three people laugh. By spring, nobody is laughing and the Tally Master has a new column.

choices.text: Eat alone, standing up

effects.log: You eat alone, standing up, where everyone can see you are not afraid to. It is very tiring.

events.text: A Hall Master's heir is holding court on the stairs, as they do, and somebody offers you a seat as a joke, to see what you will do. The tables of the Hall are not friendships. They are small armies that have not been told yet. {gn_clique} sends you a note in passing that says only, "We have noticed you also count."

choices.text: Answer {gn_clique}'s note

effects.log: You write back: "Since when?" It is apparently the correct answer. You are given a place.

choices.text: Take the seat on the stairs and do not laugh

effects.log: You sit. The joke stops being a joke quite quickly. The heir looks at you with the eyes of someone rearranging a list.

choices.text: Start a table for people the stairs have laughed at

effects.log: You find there are more of them than the stairs had thought. You find you like that very much.

choices.text: Stay with nobody, and sell what you overhear

effects.log: You go on belonging to no one. By spring, all of them are paying you a little, and none of them trusts you. That seems fair.

events.text: There is a face you know from long before the Hall. Your rival is here too, of course, and has already gathered {gn_rival_clique} around them, and there is a space at their table so exactly your size that it must have been measured. The rest of the Hall has stopped pretending not to watch. Whatever you do next, it goes in the tally twice.

choices.text: Sit down across from your rival

effects.log: You sit. Your rival passes you the salt without a word. The whole room lets out a breath, and every table moves its plans around.

choices.text: Go to {gn_clique}, and let them watch you do it

effects.log: You walk the long way round. Your rival does not look up, which is how you know.

choices.text: Set up your own table, right beside {gn_rival_clique}

effects.log: You put your bench down an arm's length from theirs. It is the most entertaining year the Hall has had since the fire.

choices.text: Eat in your cell

effects.log: You eat in your cell. Your rival sends a bowl over, with a note: "Coward. Eat." You eat.

events.text: Your mark on the tally has been rubbed out in the night, and {npc}'s chalked in where it was. That is permitted. Everything short of the one law is permitted. {npc} watches you read it, leaning on the wall, entirely at ease, because nobody dies in the Hall unless the Hall has called a trial, and {he} knows you know.

choices.text: Chalk your mark back in, and go on waiting

effects.log: You chalk it back in, smaller, and say nothing. You begin keeping a tally of your own, somewhere it cannot be rubbed out.

choices.text: Petition the Tally Master for a trial of hands

effects.log: You petition. The Tally Master looks delighted, in the way a cat is delighted. The trial is set for dawn.

choices.text: Lay the whole matter before the Tally Master

effects.log: You report it, chapter and verse. {npc} spends a month carrying water up the Ninth Stair. Nobody in the Hall calls you a coward. They just take note.

choices.text: Go after {npc} tonight, with no trial called

effects.log: There is only the one law, and you find yourself on the stair at midnight, on your way to break it.

events.text: A rumour has you selling your table's secrets to the Tally Masters. It is well made: you admire it, in a way. It took someone a season. {npc} sits down opposite you at breakfast and, very pleasantly, asks how business is. Half the room is listening. Behind {him}, a second-year has begun to shift their bench away from you.

choices.text: Finish your breakfast, and remember this

effects.log: You finish your rice to the last grain. {npc} is a little disappointed. You will not be, later.

choices.text: Call for a trial of hands, here and now, in front of the room

effects.log: You stand up and say it loud enough for the back benches. {npc} stops smiling, and starts looking forward to it.

choices.text: Show the Tally Master where the rumour started

effects.log: It takes a week to prove it and an hour to tell it. {npc} stands on the stair all night for it, and looks down at you and smiles.

choices.text: Wait for {npc} on the dark turn of the stair

effects.log: Everyone knows what happens on the dark turn of the stair. It has just never happened to someone with this many people watching.

events.text: They have announced the winter trial, and the pairs are chalked on the wall. Somebody has been paid to put you against {npc}, and {npc} has been told, and you have not. You find out when {he} bows to you across the yard before the drum. It is the small polite bow you give someone you have already beaten.

choices.text: Lose nothing that matters: hold back, watch {him}

effects.log: You give {him} the bout and take {his} whole style home with you. {npc} thinks {he} won. Let {him}.

choices.text: Fight with everything you have

effects.log: You bow back, much lower, and when the drum goes you do not hold anything back at all.

choices.text: Tell the Tally Master who was paid

effects.log: You name the chalk-boy, the price, and the day. Three people stop being friendly. One more is suddenly very friendly indeed.

choices.text: Make it the kind of bout no one gets up from

effects.log: When the drum goes, you decide the Hall can call that a trial if it likes. The Masters are faster than you had hoped.

events.text: In the last winter they clear the Ninth Stair. Everyone who is left goes up it at once, and comes down however they come down. No one is to die, and the Tally Masters stand at each landing to see to it. Whoever stands alone at the top is the {sda_title} of {gn_gen}, and all the Hall Masters in the mountains have sent someone to watch.

choices.text: Go up and do not stop

effects.log: You tie your sleeves back and go up. Below you, someone has begun taking notes.

choices.text: Bow at the bottom step, and let them go

effects.log: You bow to the stair and step aside. Everyone sees. The Hall Masters' people write that down, too, and some of them write it with interest.

events.text: The night before the Stair, {gn_room} come and sit on your mat. Nobody says much. Somebody has saved a piece of dried plum for four years for this. Tomorrow the tally closes, and everything they have written about you for four years becomes what you are. Up the mountain, you can hear them sweeping the top landing.

choices.text: Eat the plum, and be first on the stair

effects.log: It is a terrible plum, four years old. You will remember it longer than the crown, whichever way it goes.

choices.text: Say you have got what you came for, and sleep in

effects.log: You sleep until noon, for the first time in four years. Your cell, fighting on without you, thinks about that.

events.text: You turn in your tally stick at the bottom of the mountain, and the clerk reads you your own total as if it were a bill. An officer of the {sda_ladder} is waiting by the road with a black robe over one arm. "The Cult always has room for those who can count," she says. Behind you, those who kept your back are pretending to tie their boots.

choices.text: Put on the robe

effects.log: It fits. Somebody had your measurements. You stopped being surprised by that in the first year.

choices.text: Say your people come with you

effects.log: You look back at them. They stop pretending about the boots. The officer counts them, and then looks at you differently.

choices.text: Say you will go down your own road for a while

effects.log: She shrugs and folds the robe up again. "It will still fit," she says. It is not entirely a comfort.

events.text: The last morning, the chalk-boy, who is now a very old-looking twenty, washes your name off the cell door with a wet rag. That is all the ceremony there is. Outside, the road forks: down to the ranks of the {sda_ladder}, down to the world, and a third way that only makes sense if somebody is walking behind you.

choices.text: Go down to the ranks of the {sda_ladder}

effects.log: You report at noon. By evening you have a post, and an enemy, and a very clear idea of where you stand.

choices.text: Take the ones who followed you, and go home

effects.log: You walk out at the head of a very small column. The chalk-boy bows, the first time you have seen him do it for anyone.

choices.text: Take the world

effects.log: You take the road that does not go to anyone. It is much quieter than you expected.

events.text: {npc} is sitting on the wall outside your door, and {he} has brought chalk. {He} draws two strokes on the stone between you, and looks up. "We never closed this," {he} says. "No Tally Master out here. No trial. Nobody at all to stop either of us, if you have got old and careful."

choices.text: Take the chalk, and fight

effects.log: You rub out one of the strokes with your boot, and get ready.

choices.text: Tell {him} one of you will not be walking away

effects.log: {npc} looks almost happy. {He} puts the chalk away. It will not be needed.

choices.text: Rub out both strokes

effects.log: You rub them out and hold out a hand to help {him} down from the wall. {npc} stares at it for a long time.

choices.text: Say you are busy this year

effects.log: "I will write that down," says {npc}, and does. {He} is gone by morning.

events.text: The Hall taught you both the same thing, so you are not surprised to learn that {npc} has been watching your house for a month, counting who comes and goes. {He} steps out onto the road as you pass, alone, hands empty, in plain view. "I have your whole year written down," {he} says. "Shall I read it out, or shall we settle up?"

choices.text: Settle up

effects.log: You put down what you are carrying. It is, you realise, a great relief to do this honestly.

choices.text: Settle it for good

effects.log: There is nobody to stop your hand now, and you both know it. {npc} takes one step back and sets {his} feet.

choices.text: Ask {him} to read it out, and sit down to listen

effects.log: You sit on a stone. {npc} reads. Somewhere around the spring, you both start to laugh. It is over.

choices.text: Keep walking

effects.log: You keep walking. You can feel {him} write that down too.

events.text: {npc}, your Tally Master, runs the first lesson with a stick of chalk and no sword at all. "Everyone in this room will be asked to betray someone in this room," {he} says. "I want to see you work out who and why before you are asked." {He} waits. It turns out {he} means now. {He} looks at you first. The chalk does not move.

choices.text: Name someone, and give your reasons well

effects.log: You do it. It is horrible, and it is quite good. {npc} makes a mark, and the mark is for you.

choices.text: Name yourself, and give your reasons

effects.log: There is a silence. {npc} looks at you properly for the first time. "That," {he} says, "is either very stupid or the best answer I have had in nine years."

choices.text: Refuse the question

effects.log: {npc} writes something down that is not a mark. "Noted," {he} says, and moves on. You have an idea you will hear about this again.

events.text: The lesson is a run up the mountain with a stone, and at the top {npc} asks each of you to tell {him} how many stones the person ahead of you dropped. Nobody was told to count. A Tally Master's work is never the part they tell you about. You did count, a little. Beside you, a third-year cheats, smoothly, and looks at you to see if you saw.

choices.text: Report the count, and the cheating

effects.log: {npc} adds to your mark. The third-year adds to something else. You will meet again.

choices.text: Report the count, and keep the cheating to yourself

effects.log: You will collect on that later, and the third-year knows it. {npc} also knows it, and seems to approve.

choices.text: Say you were watching the road and not the people

effects.log: "Then you will be killed by people," says {npc}, not unkindly. It stays with you. You start counting.

events.text: You are sent to serve {npc}'s tea for a month. It is plainly a test, and it is plainly a test of something other than tea. In the second week you find a page left open on {his} table, with a list of first-years on it and a line through three of the names. {npc} is watching the kettle very carefully.

choices.text: Read it, and say so

effects.log: "Good," says {npc}, without turning round. "Everyone reads it. You are only the second who has told me." {He} gives you the better cup.

choices.text: Warn the three on the list

effects.log: You warn them. One thanks you. One tries to sell you to the Master. {npc} seems to find it all extremely informative.

choices.text: Turn the page over and pour the tea

effects.log: You pour. {npc} sighs a little. You have done nothing wrong, and it will not be good enough.

events.text: In your last year {npc} has you up to {his} room, the one with the window, and shows you your whole tally in {his} small handwriting. It takes a while. "There is a vow, for those who want to walk this road knowing what it costs," {he} says. "Most do not. It would make you harder to use." {He} closes the book. "That is not an argument against it."

choices.text: Swear it before {npc}

effects.log: {He} listens to the whole of it, and then writes the day down, and nothing else. It is the kindest thing you have ever seen {him} do.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the book says you are worth

effects.log: "To me?" {npc} says. {He} shows you the last line. You spend the rest of the year earning a better one.

choices.text: Thank {him} for the book, and leave it shut

effects.log: You leave without another look. You find you do not need to know, or perhaps that you would rather not.

events.text: {npc} is getting old on those stairs. You come upon {him} on the fifth landing, breathing carefully, and {he} waves you off. Then {he} says, not looking at you, "One of the houses has asked me for a list of the ones to watch. I always give them a list. I could be persuaded about what is on it. Or there is the vow, if you would rather be above all that."

choices.text: Ask {him} to put your name on it

effects.log: Your name goes on the list. It is a good thing, and it is the most dangerous thing that has ever happened to you.

choices.text: Ask {him} to hear your vow instead

effects.log: You kneel down, there on the fifth landing. {npc} gets {his} breath back to hear it. Neither of you ever mentions the list again.

choices.text: Help {him} up the stair, and do not answer

effects.log: You give {him} your arm. {He} takes it, and is annoyed, and does not let go until the top.

events.text: Once a year, by a custom no one will explain, the Hall forgets to wake you. Nobody is counting today. You and {npc} wake up to the sound of nothing, and for a while neither of you knows what to do with it. {He} finds a slope above the kitchens where the sun gets in, and says if you tell anyone, {he} will have to deny it.

choices.text: Go up and sit in the sun with {him}

effects.log: You talk about nothing, for the first time in a year. Neither of you writes any of it down, as far as you know.

choices.text: Spend the day working on your weak side

effects.log: You go down to the yard alone. It is very quiet, and you get a great deal done. {npc} does not ask you up again.

events.text: {npc} has a fever, and the Hall does not excuse fevers. You are not friends, exactly. People here are not. But you are the one who wakes to hear {him} shaking on {his} mat at the worst hour of the night, and the Tally Masters are not about, and if {he} misses the morning count, it is {his} mark that goes.

choices.text: Answer the morning count in {his} voice

effects.log: You have listened to {him} for a year. You do it well. The Tally Master looks at you for a long moment, then moves on. {npc} never says thank you. {He} just starts saving you the good end of the bread.

choices.text: Let the morning decide

effects.log: You lie down again. {npc} loses the mark. It is nothing to do with you, as {he} will agree with you in the morning, very politely.

events.text: First snow. Somebody on the fourth landing starts it, and within minutes every student in the Hall Below the Throne, all those future enemies, is throwing snow as hard as they can at the nearest Hall Master's heir. {npc} hits you in the ear. For about as long as it takes the Tally Masters to get down the stairs, nobody is anything but sixteen.

choices.text: Get {him} back, properly

effects.log: You put a great deal of snow down the back of {his} robe. {He} shrieks. Nobody will ever believe it happened. You keep it, though.

choices.text: Use the confusion to read the Tally Master's book

effects.log: You have about four minutes. You learn a great deal. You are also, somehow, very much alone when the bell goes.

events.text: A visitor to the Hall. {npc} walks the third-year yard with {his} hands behind {his} back and speaks to no one, and everyone trains a little harder. You know a Hall Master's people when you see them. That evening {he} stops by you, the way you stop by a horse. "My Master keeps a hall of a thousand," {he} says. "It has room near the top for someone who knows who {he} owes. Think quickly."

choices.text: Say you know who you would owe

effects.log: {npc} nods, once. It is the beginning of a very long debt. It is also a great deal of protection.

choices.text: Say you will owe nobody before you must

effects.log: "Then you will be owed nothing," says {npc}, and moves on to the next one. {He} does not look back. It stings a little.

events.text: A letter, and {npc} who brings it, a quiet person from the Hall of Tallies with very clean hands. Somebody in the great halls has been reading the tally from a distance and has picked you out from it. You are to be sponsored. All it needs is your mark. It is the sort of thing that people here would poison each other for. You wonder who is watching you read it.

choices.text: Put your mark on it

effects.log: You sign. {npc} blows on the ink. Your name now sits in somebody's plans, and you are no longer quite your own.

choices.text: Hand it back with thanks

effects.log: {npc} takes it back without a flicker. A thing like that does not come twice. You sleep unusually well.

events.text: {npc} of {sda_house} comes up the mountain with gifts for the Tally Masters and a sharp look for you. "The other houses have had their people in this Hall since you came," {he} says quietly. "Their heirs have sides already. You have a table and a blanket. Let me put you in the way of people who matter, and let your house remember who did it."

choices.text: Tell {him} to go ahead

effects.log: You are moved, on a board you can only partly see. Back at your house, someone is pleased. It feels like being picked up.

choices.text: Say you will make your side here, on your own

effects.log: {npc} sniffs. "With a blanket," {he} says, and goes off to report you. But you notice that your table is listening.

events.text: An old clerk of the Hall finds you, wherever you are, years after. {sda_teacher}'s tally, he says, has you down as owing. A Hall Master who spent marks on you wants a small service in return, the sort nobody puts on paper, or silver instead: {sda_cost} taels. He has a small book, and shows you the page. It adds up. It always does.

choices.text: Pay in silver: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You count it out. He gives you a receipt, the first you have ever seen from the Cult, and you keep it.

choices.text: Do the service

effects.log: You ask no more than you need to know, and you go to do it.

choices.text: Tell him the tally is closed

effects.log: He closes the book without complaint. You have a feeling someone will be along.

events.text: You are at dinner when a black robe sits down across from you and starts on your rice. "Your marks were a loan," she says. "The Hall lent you a name when you were sixteen. It would like it paid back. {sda_cost} taels, or there is a door that needs opening in a town a long way from here." She finishes the bowl. "You always did keep count. So did we."

choices.text: Put the silver on the table: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: She counts it twice, nods, and leaves you the empty bowl.

choices.text: Ask which door

effects.log: She tells you. You pay for dinner.

choices.text: Tell her to send someone better

effects.log: "Oh, we shall," she says, quite pleasantly, and goes.

events.text: There is a line in {sda_teacher}'s handwriting, delivered by a stranger, that says only your name, a sum and a question mark. {sda_cost} taels, or a job. It is the question mark you keep looking at. {sda_teacher} never once in all those years wrote down anything {sda_teacher} was not sure of. You think this may be the nearest thing to a courtesy the Hall has ever shown you.

choices.text: Send the silver

effects.log: You send it, and a note with it that just says: "Closed?" No answer comes, which is an answer.

choices.text: Go and do what is asked

effects.log: You read the rest of the note. It is not a very nice job. You go.

choices.text: Send back the note, with the question mark circled

effects.log: It amuses you for about a month. Then a stranger starts asking after you in the market.

events.text: A black-robed {npc}, older, wider, sits down on your bench uninvited and steals your bread with exactly the same hand. "You owe me a blanket," {he} says. It has been years. You have both done things. {He} wants nothing at all, {he} says, and it takes you most of the evening to believe {him}, and even then you count your silver afterwards.

choices.text: Send out for more bread

effects.log: You talk till the lamp goes out, and you tell {him} more than you should. So does {he}.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} really came for

effects.log: {npc} sighs and puts the bread down. "Nothing," {he} says. "But I see the Hall worked." {He} leaves.

events.text: Word reaches you, by a roundabout road: {npc} of your old cell has been asking questions about you in the great halls. You find {him} before {he} finds you. {He} only laughs. It seems {he} has been steering a little trouble away from your door, the way you do for someone who once knew your worst habits. "I have kept a tally," {he} says. "You are behind."

choices.text: Ask what you owe, and pay it

effects.log: It is a very small sum, and it is not silver. You pay it gladly, and you are both a little embarrassed.

choices.text: Tell {him} you never asked {him} to

effects.log: "No," says {npc}. "That is why it counts." {He} goes. You find you are a little less safe than you were.

events.text: {npc} has come to tell you who else is left from your year. It takes about as long as a cup of tea. Some are Hall Masters now. Some are lines in a book. {He} reads them off without any expression at all, and at the end {he} looks at you and says "And us," and neither of you can think of a joke.

choices.text: Drink to the ones in the book

effects.log: You drink. You find you remember all of their faces, even the ones you hated. Especially those.

choices.text: Ask which of the Hall Masters can be moved

effects.log: {npc} tells you. Of course you asked, and of course {he} knew you would. It is the last visit, you think.

events.text: The children have begun to circle the seat, and {npc} of your old cell has come up the mountain to ask you, frankly, which of them {he} ought to stand behind. {He} has people in the halls now. {He} also has a very long memory for who kept the good blanket. "Say a name," {he} says, "or say nothing, and I shall do what I think best."

choices.text: Say {sda_side}'s name

effects.log: {npc} nods. "That one is already strong," {he} says. "I will make it stronger. I do hope you know what you are doing."

choices.text: Name the one with the fewest friends

effects.log: {npc} raises an eyebrow. "You always did like a hard climb." {He} goes to find the child nobody else is courting.

choices.text: Tell {him} to stay out of it

effects.log: "From you, that is new," says {npc}, and stays out of it. For now. {He} did not say how long.

events.text: There is a tally of the heirs going round the Hall Below the Throne these days. The students keep it for practice. {npc}, who taught you to read such things, brings you a copy. {He} has thoughts. {He} and three more of your year could make one side very hard to beat, with one word from you. {He} is watching your face like the old days.

choices.text: Give {him} {sda_side}, and let the tally shift

effects.log: The tally does shift, by morning. You notice you do not feel any better for it.

choices.text: Send {him} to the one the tally has forgotten

effects.log: That child climbs a good way up the page, and somebody in a far hall starts sweating.

choices.text: Tell {him} the children can do their own counting

effects.log: {npc} smiles and tucks the copy away. "That is what they will say about you, too," {he} says.

events.text: A plain parcel reaches you from the mountains. {sda_teacher} has died, at a great age, on the stairs, still teaching. Inside there is a stick of chalk worn down to a stub and your own tally page, in that small hand, cut from the book. Someone has added a last line at the bottom. It is the only time you have ever seen {sda_teacher}'s writing go crooked. It says: "Enough."

choices.text: Keep the page

effects.log: You keep it in the drawer with the things that do not need to be counted any more.

choices.text: Burn the page and keep the chalk

effects.log: You burn it, and find a use for the chalk. It writes very well. You draw a line under something.

events.text: An Acolyte with a lamp stands in the doorway at the hour before dawn, and does not knock. "The School under the Altar has been keeping a place," she says, "since before any family you know of had a name." She says it the way people mention the weather. Then she waits. The lamp does not flicker, though there is a wind.

choices.text: Follow the lamp

effects.log: You do not pack. She tells you there is no need. You think about that all the way down.

choices.text: Say your place can go on being kept

effects.log: She bows. "It will," she says, and you see, with a small coldness, that she means it.

events.text: They read out your name at the evening verse. You are not there, you are three valleys away, and you hear about it from a pedlar who will not meet your eye. In the morning there is a bowl outside your door, a plain clay one, very old, with your name scratched in the bottom in a hand nobody has written for centuries. It has always, it seems, been your bowl.

choices.text: Carry the bowl to the Altar

effects.log: It is heavier than it looks. People step off the road for you, and you did not ask them to.

choices.text: Break the bowl on the doorstep

effects.log: It breaks. A week later there is another one. You stop going out by that door. After a while they stop coming.

events.text: A Master of the Blood Hall has come to look at you in person, which is not done. {sda_School} takes the children of the Cult at fifteen, and has done it the same way for six hundred years. "There is no examination," the Master says. "You have been examined. You may decline. It has been done. I can tell you their names, if you like."

choices.text: Go down with the Master

effects.log: "Good," says the Master, and you feel relieved, and then you wonder who taught you to feel that.

choices.text: Ask for the names

effects.log: The Master recites eleven of them, gently. You decide you would still prefer not to. The Master bows and leaves you to your life.

events.text: You sleep under the long stair, on a stone with the shape of other sleepers worn into it. There are four hollows. The lamps of the first landing must be lit before the verse, and whoever lights them first is who the rest follow, and it has been so for longer than the Cult has had a name. {npc} is already holding the taper out towards you, unlit, to see what you do. {gn_room} watch.

choices.text: Take the taper out of {his} hand

effects.log: You take it. There is no struggle at first. {npc} simply closes {his} hand again, and the struggle comes in the dark, without a sound.

choices.text: Kneel, and let {npc} light the first lamp

effects.log: You kneel. It is surprisingly easy. It frightens you afterwards, how easy it was.

choices.text: Keep your own hollow and speak to no one

effects.log: You lie down in the coldest hollow. The stone remembers somebody who was taller. You begin the long work of saying nothing.

events.text: The first verse takes three hours. Nobody explains the words. They are older than the words you know. {npc}, next to you on the kneeling row, begins on the second night to add a small note of {his} own to the end of each line, and the others, one by one, begin to follow {him}. {gn_room} are doing it now. Nobody has said anything. Everyone is waiting to see whether you will.

choices.text: Sing your own note over {his}

effects.log: It is a very quiet war, fought entirely in the throat. You win the first night. Neither of you can speak the next day.

choices.text: Follow {his} note, and do it well

effects.log: Your voice settles under {his}. {npc} glances sideways, and something is decided.

choices.text: Say the verse exactly as it was taught

effects.log: You say it as written. It is lonely. A Master of the Blood Hall, passing behind you in the dark, pauses for just a moment.

events.text: There is an old bowl for each hollow, and at dusk the Acolytes fill them with the School's bitter red tea, which is not to be spoken of and which you can taste for hours. Tonight there are four hollows and only three bowls. {npc} is holding {his} and looking at you over the rim. {gn_room} have stopped drinking. The Acolytes are already gone.

choices.text: Take {his} bowl

effects.log: You do not spill any of it. That turns out to be the part that matters. The others move their mats a little towards yours.

choices.text: Go without tonight, and tell {npc} it is {his} due

effects.log: {npc} drinks without taking {his} eyes off you. Tomorrow there are four bowls again. You are the one who remembers why.

choices.text: Pour yours out on the stone for whoever slept here first

effects.log: Nobody has ever done that, as far as you know. The stone drinks it. Nobody sits near you for a month.

events.text: In your second year you are permitted to learn that the students have orders of their own, older than the Masters' patience. They do not call them orders. They call them {gn_clique} and other names that mean nothing. One of them has begun to leave a place for you on the kneeling row. There is another that does not leave places. People merely find themselves in it.

choices.text: Kneel in the place {gn_clique} has left you

effects.log: You kneel. Someone beside you starts the verse on your breath. You are now, you gather, one of them.

choices.text: Go to the strongest and kneel behind them

effects.log: You kneel at their backs until they notice. It takes all winter. You do not mind. You have started not to mind things.

choices.text: Light a lamp of your own, and see who comes

effects.log: You light it on the lowest stair, where it is forbidden by nobody, because nobody ever thought of it. Three people come. Then five.

choices.text: Keep to no order

effects.log: You keep to none. It is not safer. It is only quieter.

events.text: An old Acolyte tells you, without being asked, that {gn_clique} has existed for four hundred years and has been the wrong side for all of them. He seems to think that this is a recommendation. Nobody here is ever in a hurry. The feuds between the orders were old when the village you come from was a marsh. You are, he explains, simply this century's turn.

choices.text: Take your turn with {gn_clique}

effects.log: You learn their small sign. It is nothing but a way of folding the left sleeve. You will do it until you die.

choices.text: Ask him which order has never been the wrong side

effects.log: He shows you, smiling very gently. You go to them. They do not smile at all.

choices.text: Tell him this century will have a new one

effects.log: He looks at you for a long while. "It has been tried," he says. "I will show you where they are buried, if you win."

choices.text: Thank him, and fold your sleeve your own way

effects.log: You fold it your own way. Everyone notices. Nobody comments. It goes on being noticed for four years.

events.text: You did not expect your rival to come here, down the long stair. But there they are on the far side of the kneeling row, in a crimson sash, with {gn_rival_clique} folded around them, and they turn and nod to you across the lamps. It is a very calm nod. You feel it is the first truly frightening thing they have ever done.

choices.text: Go and kneel beside your rival

effects.log: You walk the whole length of the row to do it. Your rival moves a little, to give you room. "It is better down here," they whisper, and you are not sure which of you they mean.

choices.text: Join {gn_clique} instead

effects.log: You kneel with your own kind. Across the lamps, your rival keeps watching. They have a great deal of patience, now.

choices.text: Light your own lamp, across from theirs

effects.log: Two lamps, one row. The Masters say nothing. The Masters, you begin to suspect, are enjoying themselves.

choices.text: Look away, and go on with the verse

effects.log: You say your verse. You can feel their nod on the side of your face until spring.

events.text: You have begun hearing your name in the evening verse, in a place where no name goes. It is {npc}, three along. {He} does not raise {his} voice or look at you. Nobody has said what it does to have your name in the verse. People around you are starting to leave a little more room. And there is one law: no hand is raised in sight of the lamps.

choices.text: Bear it, and learn the verse better than {he} does

effects.log: You bear it. You spend the nights on the old words. You will have a use for them one day.

choices.text: Ask {him} to walk out past the last lamp

effects.log: The dark past the last lamp is the only place in the School where a thing can be settled. {npc} inclines {his} head. {He} had been hoping you would ask.

choices.text: Lay it before the Master of the Blood Hall

effects.log: The Master listens, and has {npc} moved to the far end of the row. Then the Master looks at you, thoughtful, as if for the first time, and asks to hear the verse again.

choices.text: Raise your hand to {him} where {he} kneels

effects.log: It is very quiet on the row. You stand up. No one has done this in your lifetime, and you are about to learn why.

events.text: Your bowl has been moved. It is a small thing. Each morning it is a little further down the row, towards the low door where the Acolytes take what is left. Nobody ever sees who does it. On the ninth morning {npc} catches your eye, and very slightly lifts {his} own bowl to you. You know what is on the other side of the low door. Everyone does, more or less.

choices.text: Carry your bowl back each morning, without a word

effects.log: You carry it back. Every morning, for a year. It becomes a sort of conversation. You find that you are both getting better at it.

choices.text: Meet {him} past the last lamp and have it out

effects.log: You find {him} in the dark with your hands open, and {he} sets {his} bowl down carefully first.

choices.text: Tell an Acolyte, and ask who holds the book of bowls

effects.log: There is, it turns out, a book of bowls. {npc}'s is moved instead, one place, then two. {He} bows to you very deeply the next time you pass.

choices.text: Bring your bowl down on {his} head at the verse

effects.log: You stand up with the bowl in your hands, in front of every lamp in the School.

events.text: The Masters have set the two of you to tend the same lamp through the long winter fast, and it is not a coincidence, because nothing here is. {npc} sits an arm's length off, very still. {He} has decided that one of you will let it go out and be blamed. For seven nights neither of you has slept more than an hour. {He} is, you are beginning to think, not as tired as you are.

choices.text: Stay awake, and let {him} see you do it

effects.log: You hold on through the fast by not blinking, more or less. The lamp stays lit. You will not forgive {him} the seven nights.

choices.text: Say you will fight {him} past the last lamp when it is over

effects.log: "If you can stand," says {npc}. Both of you are shaking with hunger on the day. It is the most honest fight you will ever have.

choices.text: Call a Master and hand back the lamp

effects.log: You give it up in front of the Master. It is not cowardice, you explain. {npc} has been dozing with {his} eyes open since the third night. You saw. So does the Master, now.

choices.text: Put {his} hand in the flame, and end it

effects.log: Something old and tired in you has had enough. You reach across the lamp.

events.text: In the last year comes the Long Kneeling. Every student left in the School kneels before the great lamp and holds their art up against all the others, without moving, without a word, from dusk until someone can bear no more, and then the next. Those who rise are led away, gently. The last upright is the {sda_title}, of {gn_gen}. The Elders of the Altar have come down to see.

choices.text: Kneel, and hold

effects.log: You kneel. You have been practising this for four years without being told. It occurs to you that was the whole School.

choices.text: Bow to the lamp, and rise before it begins

effects.log: You rise before the first breath of it. An Elder turns her old head to watch you go, with what you could almost take for interest.

events.text: {gn_room} are with you under the stair on the last night. Nobody has anything to say, after four years. A Master of the Blood Hall comes by with the lamp, and looks at you each in turn. "The one who wins this," the Master says, "will be spoken of here for six hundred years, along with all the others, whose names you have never heard." The lamp moves on.

choices.text: Be spoken of

effects.log: You lie awake, working out what that means, and you decide to go through with it anyway.

choices.text: Decide you would rather be alive and unmentioned

effects.log: You sleep. In the morning you kneel with the rest and stand up early, and a great weight goes off you. Nobody remarks on it.

events.text: At the top of the long stair, they hand you back your shoes. A captain of the {sda_ladder} is waiting there in the bright daylight, which hurts. "They say you can hold still," she says. "There is work for that." The ones who knelt beside you are coming up the stair behind you, one step at a time, without being told to.

choices.text: Take the crimson robe

effects.log: You take it. It smells of the same lamps. You had thought that part would be over.

choices.text: Turn and hold out your hand to those behind you

effects.log: They take it, one by one. The captain looks away. People have, you are finding, begun to do that.

choices.text: Put on your shoes and walk

effects.log: You walk. The light gets easier in a day or two. The verse takes a good deal longer.

events.text: No one comes to see you off. There is an old custom: you say your own name once at the last lamp, out loud, so that the School can forget it. Your voice sounds strange. Behind you the evening verse has begun without you, and it sounds no different. Then the Acolyte holds up three things, without speaking: a crimson sash, a list of those who would follow you, and your shoes.

choices.text: Take the sash, and go to the {sda_ladder}

effects.log: You report to the {sda_ladder} at sundown. They already know how you take your tea.

choices.text: Take the list

effects.log: There are not many names. You know each voice. You go up together, and you do not speak until you reach the grass.

choices.text: Take your shoes

effects.log: You take your shoes. They no longer fit. You walk out in them anyway, on principle.

events.text: You hear it from three streets off. Someone is saying the evening verse, here, in the open air, in a market town, and at the end of each line is your name. {npc} is sitting by the well with {his} eyes closed. {He} finishes the line before {he} opens them. "No lamps," {he} says. "I have looked. Not one in the whole town."

choices.text: Walk out past the last house and have it out

effects.log: You nod towards the fields. {npc} rises, as easily as if {he} had been kneeling for a day and a night. {He} probably has.

choices.text: End the verse

effects.log: Nobody is watching here, and nothing is keeping the old law. You take off your coat.

choices.text: Say the closing words of a matter

effects.log: They are very old words. You did not know that you remembered them. {npc} stops in the middle of a breath.

choices.text: Walk on

effects.log: You walk on. It follows you for a street or two, and then it does not. Your name will be back.

events.text: A clay bowl turns up on your table, cracked, very old, with your name in the bottom. You had forgotten that feeling. {npc} is in the doorway behind you, and {he} has been there for some time. "They moved mine, too, in the end," {he} says. "Down to the low door. I went through it, and I came back." {He} does not look as though {he} came back all the way.

choices.text: Pick up the bowl and step outside with {him}

effects.log: You put the bowl carefully on the sill. You will want it later, whichever way this goes.

choices.text: Crack it the rest of the way, and go for {him}

effects.log: It breaks in two on the table. {npc} smiles and sets {his} feet, and it is not a good smile.

choices.text: Fill it, and hold it out to {him}

effects.log: You pour tea into a broken bowl. It runs out over your hand. {npc} looks at that for a long, long time, then bows.

choices.text: Tell {him} to come back when {he} is all here

effects.log: It is the cruellest thing you could have said. {npc} goes. You keep the bowl. You do not really know why.

events.text: {npc}, a Master of the Blood Hall, teaches sitting down, in a voice you have to lean in for. Tonight there is a row of bowls of the bitter red tea, and {he} tells you what no one else will: it opens the old paths faster than anything does. It also takes something, and {he} has never been able to say quite what. "I have had a great many cups," {npc} says. "I do not recall the name of my mother."

choices.text: Take the cup

effects.log: It is warm. Your hands feel stronger almost at once. You try to think of something you might have forgotten, and of course you cannot.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {his} mother would have said

effects.log: A long silence. "That," {npc} says, "is the first interesting thing anyone has said in this room since the old Blood God died." {He} does not give you a cup. {He} gives you a book.

choices.text: Push the bowl back along the row

effects.log: {npc} nods, without any disappointment at all. "There will be another," {he} says. "There always is."

events.text: You spend the whole of the spring being taught to breathe, by {npc}, who corrects you with one dry finger under your ribs. The art is called something very long. You will learn it long after everyone who could tell you what it is for has died, {he} says. "I do not know what it does. My Master did not know. It is simply very, very old, and it wants students." {He} seems to think this is an adequate reason.

choices.text: Give yourself to it

effects.log: By the summer your breath moves things it did not move before. There is a second cup, on the sill, that you had not asked for. You take it.

choices.text: Learn it, and ask questions {he} cannot answer

effects.log: {npc} starts staying late, trying to answer them. It may be the first thing {he} has wanted in decades.

choices.text: Do what you are told, and keep something back

effects.log: You do it, with a small part of you shut in a room. {npc} presses a finger under your ribs, right there, and looks at you, and lets it be.

events.text: Beneath the long stair, there is another stair. {npc} takes you down it with a single lamp, past a hall of painted doors, to a wall of names cut so deep and so close together that it reads like a texture. "Everyone who ever finished," {he} says. "Find the one below which you would like to be." It is very quiet. The last name was cut quite recently, and you know who it is.

choices.text: Find your place, and put your hand on it

effects.log: You put your hand there. It is warm, which is impossible. {npc} says it is always warm. There is a cup on the way back up, and you take it.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone has ever had their name cut out

effects.log: "Three," says {npc}, and {he} shows you the hollows. You look at those for a long time. You feel a good deal better, and you do not tell {him} that.

choices.text: Say you would like to go back up now

effects.log: You are very polite about it. {npc} takes you up. You hear {him} sigh, on about the third landing, like an old door.

events.text: In your last winter, {npc} is having trouble with the stairs. {He} has you bring {his} tea to {him} now, and one evening {he} forgets your name, and looks at you with quiet interest until {he} finds it. "There is a vow," {he} says, "if you wish a thing in your life that is your own to keep. The School will not hold you to it. That is rather the point. Or there is another cup. There is always another cup."

choices.text: Swear the vow, with {npc} to hear it

effects.log: You say it. {He} listens with {his} eyes shut and asks you to say it again, and you realise {he} wishes to remember it, and that it may not be possible.

choices.text: Take the cup

effects.log: It no longer tastes of anything. You notice that, and then you notice you have stopped noticing.

choices.text: Tell {him} that {his} mother's name was probably a good one

effects.log: It is a stupid thing to say. {npc}'s hand closes on your wrist for a moment, very lightly. Then {he} goes on with {his} tea.

events.text: {npc} gives you the last lesson in the kneeling hall, when everyone else has gone. It is a form of the old art that {he} says has no name and no use, and that {he} had it from {his} Master who had it from a person who had been a child when the Altar was built. {He} moves through it once, like water finding a level. "Now you," {he} says. "It is all I have left. I would like somebody to have it."

choices.text: Learn it, and thank {him} by name

effects.log: It takes until dawn. {He} seems very moved that you know {his} name, and you wonder how many people still do.

choices.text: Swear your vow on it, so that it stays clean

effects.log: You kneel to do it. {npc} blinks at you, slow and old. "No one has ever kept a thing clean down here," {he} says. "Try."

choices.text: Say that some things should be allowed to end

effects.log: {npc} considers it for a long time, without anger. "Yes," {he} says. "That is what I would have said, I think, once." {He} teaches it to someone else.

events.text: Once in your second year they send you and {npc} up the long stair for lamp oil. It is the first daylight you have seen in months. There is a goat on the path. It has no idea what you are. {npc} stands looking at it with {his} hands hanging down, and you can see {him} remembering something, and you cannot tell what.

choices.text: Sit down on the path and stay a while

effects.log: You stay till the light goes long. The goat eats {npc}'s sash. {He} laughs, a rusty sound, and then looks around as if someone might have heard.

choices.text: Get the oil and go back down

effects.log: The School is waiting, and you find you want to be under the stone again. That frightens you, so you do not mention it. {npc} comes after you, last, still looking back.

events.text: It is a feast day, for someone. Nobody remembers who. The Acolytes bring around a sticky cake that has been made the same way for five hundred years and tastes like it. {npc} has saved half of {his} and is holding it out to you in the dark under the stair. There is no reason for it that you can think of. Nothing here happens with no reason.

choices.text: Take it, and tell {him} something true

effects.log: You tell {him} the name of the village you came from. {He} tells you {his}. You both say them over a few times, to be sure.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} wants for it

effects.log: "Nothing," says {npc}, and eats it {him}self, quite slowly. You have the feeling you have failed something, and that it was not the School's test.

events.text: You wake to find {npc} sitting up in {his} hollow in the dark, whispering. It is not the verse. It takes you a while to make it out. {He} is saying over a list: {his} sister's name, the colour of a door, the words to a stupid song about a duck. {He} sees you are awake. "I check them," {he} says. "Every night. Somebody took something, and I want to know when." It is very cold.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you the song about the duck

effects.log: It is a very stupid song. You both know it by the end of the week. You will know it when you have forgotten your own face.

choices.text: Tell {him} to go to sleep before the Masters hear

effects.log: {npc} looks at you and then lies down. You listen to {him} not sleeping, and you start making a list of your own, very quietly.

events.text: {npc}, an Elder of the Altar's own steward, has come down to the School with a cold and a great many keys. {He} stops at the end of your row while you are kneeling and stands there for an hour. Afterwards an Acolyte brings you a key on a red thread. It opens one of the lower halls. "The Elder would have you near," the Acolyte says. "You may return it. It has been done."

choices.text: Put the thread around your neck

effects.log: {npc} nods from far away. Something large has noticed you. It will not be easy to be unnoticed again.

choices.text: Give the key back to {npc} with both hands

effects.log: You do it correctly, which is a thing that matters here. {npc} takes it with a small cold bow, and looks at you for a moment as one looks at a door that has stuck.

events.text: A stranger comes to the School, and it is {npc}, and {he} is the first person you have met in three years who seems to be in a hurry. "The Blood God's Herald keeps a hall for promising youngsters," {he} says. "Your name came up. It is a good hall. Most of them come out again." {He} looks over {his} shoulder as {he} says it. In this place. Whatever {he} is afraid of, you would like to know.

choices.text: Accept, and ask what {he} is afraid of

effects.log: {He} gives a short laugh, signs you in, and does not answer. But you have a patron now, and that is an answer of its kind.

choices.text: Say you would rather finish here first

effects.log: {npc} shrugs and hurries off. Later you ask an Acolyte about the Herald's hall. The Acolyte says nothing, and adds another lamp to your landing.

events.text: {npc} comes every year for the Long Kneeling, and has for thirty years, and sits with {his} chin on {his} hand as if it were theatre. This year {he} has you brought over between the verses. "I can do you a great deal of good," {he} says. "You will not like what I ask of you, in the end. None of them have. They all say it was worth it, though, the ones who can still say things."

choices.text: Say that you are willing to find out

effects.log: {He} smiles for the first time. It is a very good smile, and it has clearly been kept in a box.

choices.text: Say you can do without that kind of good

effects.log: {npc} is not at all offended. "Ask me again when you are forty," {he} says, and goes back to watching.

events.text: The bowl has come back, the very old one, carried by an Acolyte who has walked a long way in thin shoes. The Altar School keeps count of what it pours, she explains, and yours has come due. There is a service, or the School will take {sda_cost} taels for its lamps. {sda_teacher} kept your account, she says, as far as {sda_teacher} could remember it. She looks at your hands while she says it.

choices.text: Pay for the lamps: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: She takes the silver without counting, and she takes the bowl too. You did not expect to feel that.

choices.text: Do the service

effects.log: It is a small thing to do, she says. You go and do it. You do not sleep well for a good while afterwards.

choices.text: Tell her the Altar can come and get it

effects.log: She bows. She has never been told anything else that interested her. Someone else will walk here in thin shoes, and they will not be carrying a bowl.

events.text: You wake in the night saying a line of the evening verse, and you do not know how long you have been at it. In the morning there is a note: the cups you took were not given, they were lent, and the Masters of the Blood Hall would like to speak of how you will pay it. {sda_cost} taels would light the lamps for a good long while. Or there is something they would like you to carry somewhere.

choices.text: Send the silver: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You send it. The verse does not stop at once, but it gets quieter. Some of it is even yours.

choices.text: Carry what they ask

effects.log: It is quite a small box. You do not ask. You carry it a long way.

choices.text: Refuse, in your own words, not theirs

effects.log: It takes you a whole morning to find any words that are only yours. You send them. An answer comes in the form of a person.

events.text: Somebody is cutting your name. A Blood Acolyte in the market tells you this very softly, and then buys some turnips. On the deep wall beneath the Altar, she says, the School is cutting you in among those who finished. They have stopped halfway. It costs {sda_cost} taels to have them go on, or one job. It costs more, she says, if they have to go on without you.

choices.text: Pay the mason's fee: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You hand it over among the turnips. It is the strangest thing you have ever bought, and you think of it often.

choices.text: Take the job

effects.log: She tells you, and buys an onion. You go and do what she has told you.

choices.text: Tell her to leave it half cut

effects.log: She looks at you with real respect. "Three," she says. "Would make four." Then someone starts to follow you home.

events.text: You know {npc} by the stillness. {He} is kneeling at the side of the road when you pass, with nothing around {him}, as if it were the lowest step of the long stair. It has been years. "I still say it," {he} says, without looking up. "The duck. Every night." {He} sings a line of it, cracked and tuneless, and you find you are smiling, and that it hurts.

choices.text: Kneel down beside {him} and sing the next line

effects.log: You sing it. A passing carter gives you both a very strange look. It is the best hour you have had in years.

choices.text: Tell {him} to get up, you are both past all that

effects.log: {npc} gets up without argument and looks at you. You have forgotten something, you can see. {He} goes on checking you, on {his} list. Then {he} goes.

events.text: {npc} has done very well, in the crimson robe. There are people behind {him} who keep their eyes down. {He} sends them off with a finger and sits with you, and {he} has become very calm and very pleasant, and when you laugh about the old stone hollows, {he} waits a moment, watching how you do it, and then laughs too. It is a very good copy.

choices.text: Say {his} village's name to {him}

effects.log: For a moment nothing happens. Then, somewhere a long way behind {his} eyes, someone looks up. {He} takes your hand and does not seem to know why.

choices.text: Talk business, and go home

effects.log: You talk business. {He} is very good at it. You get a fair price, and you go home and check your own list, which you find has got shorter.

events.text: A very old bowl comes, by a very long road, from {npc}, whom you last saw on the long stair. No note. It has been filled with river sand and has a single dried flower in it, a stupid ordinary one, from the slope with the goat. You are surprised by how long you stand holding it. You had thought all of that was gone.

choices.text: Send a bowl back with something in it

effects.log: You think for some days about what to put in it. In the end you send a duck carved out of wood, badly, by you.

choices.text: Put it on a high shelf

effects.log: You put it where you do not have to look at it, and you do not look at it, with some effort, for years.

events.text: {npc} has come up to you, in crimson, unhurried, to tell you how long the Elders of the Altar expect the children to live. {He} does it kindly. {He} knelt beside you, once, and {he} would like to do you this one service: tell {him} which of them is yours to keep, and {he} and the others from under the stair will kneel behind that one, and no one else.

choices.text: Name {sda_side}

effects.log: {npc} inclines {his} head. "That one is already burning bright," {he} says. "We will bring oil."

choices.text: Name the child no one kneels behind

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a time, and something in {his} old calm shifts. "Well," {he} says. "A lamp on the lowest stair." {He} goes.

choices.text: Tell {him} none of them should be kept like that

effects.log: "Not one has ever said so and held to it," says {npc}. "But I will wait to see." It is, you think, a form of love, down there.

events.text: The evening verse has a new line, your people tell you, and it names your heirs, in an order, and {npc} has come to ask if you wish to correct it. {He} has friends on the row. An order said at the Altar long enough stops being a guess. It is one word from you, between the two of you, who once went hungry on the same stone.

choices.text: Leave {sda_side} at the head of the line

effects.log: You say nothing, which is what the word is. {npc} nods. That night, the verse goes on as before.

choices.text: Move the last name to the first

effects.log: {npc} raises {his} eyes to you, very slowly. "That will be noticed," {he} says. You can hear how much {he} is looking forward to it.

choices.text: Have the whole line taken out

effects.log: {npc} says it cannot be done. Then {he} says it has been done, once. Then {he} goes away to see about it, and you do not hear of it again.

events.text: An Acolyte stops at your gate, thin shoes, long road. {sda_teacher} has gone through the low door. It was very peaceful, she says. At the end {sda_teacher} did not remember the Altar, the School, or the art, or any of the six hundred years. "But there was a name," she says. "Over and over. We looked it up, and we think it may be yours." She bows. She has a long walk back.

choices.text: Say the name of {sda_teacher} aloud, once, at your own lamp

effects.log: You say it. You light your lamp and let it burn the night. You do not know who else remembers that name. You are fairly sure no one does.

choices.text: Thank her, and give her better shoes

effects.log: You give her your own. She looks at them for a long time. It seems nobody has done this in six hundred years, either.

events.text: A very polite old person comes to your door at dusk, holding an unlit lantern, and asks if this is the house where you live. You say it is. They seem glad. "The School of the Unlit Lantern has room this year," they say. "It has rather a lot of room. The city is mostly empty, you see. You would be most welcome." They hold the lantern out, and do not seem to mind how long you take.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Take the lantern

effects.log: It weighs almost nothing. The old person smiles, and says the road is easy to find, and when you look up they have gone.

choices.text: Thank them, and say not this year

effects.log: "Of course," they say, and bow. "We will not trouble you. We do not trouble people." You find that they are entirely sincere, and you lock the door anyway.

events.text: Somebody has left a paper boat on your windowsill, and inside it a slip with your name and a date, in the elegant hand they use for grave-tablets. You ask around, and an old woman at the well tells you very cheerfully that it is a school. They only write to people who have stopped being frightened of something. She asks if you would like some turnips, and then she asks what it was.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Go at the date on the slip

effects.log: You go on the day. You keep the boat in your sleeve. You are not sure what it was that you stopped being frightened of, but you would like to find out.

choices.text: Put the boat on the river

effects.log: You set it on the water and watch it go. It is a very well made boat. You feel you have been rude.

events.text: The Keepers of the ghost city send for the young of the sect at fifteen, as they always have, with a note of great courtesy that is quite impossible to refuse without feeling you have kicked somebody's grandmother. "We hope you will consider joining us," it says, "for the next four years, or longer." Someone has underlined "or longer" very lightly in pencil, then rubbed it out.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Write back and accept, as politely as you can

effects.log: You write three drafts. In the end you just say yes, and thank you. A reply comes at once, thanking you for your thanks.

choices.text: Write back and decline, as politely as you can

effects.log: You decline with enormous care. A reply comes at once, thanking you for your thoughtfulness. You feel like an absolute monster for a month.

events.text: You are given a dead merchant's house to share. It has seven rooms, only one of which has a roof, and a family altar still set for dinner. {npc} is standing in the doorway of the room with the roof with {his} lantern in {his} hand, not going in, not going away, and looking at you. {gn_room} are also looking at you. It is all very courteous. Outside, it begins to rain.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Bow to {npc} and walk in ahead of {him}

effects.log: You bow as low as you can and walk straight past. {npc} is too well brought up to do anything about it until after dark.

choices.text: Hold the door for {npc}

effects.log: {He} goes in, and {he} leaves you exactly enough of the floor. It is a lesson in something.

choices.text: Go and sit under the rafters, and watch the rain

effects.log: You get extremely wet. You also get a very good view of the whole street. Something at the far end of it stops to look back at you, and then goes on.

events.text: Each house in the ghost city has its old family, and the students are expected to tend them: to dust the tablets, and to set out rice on the proper days. Somebody must keep the household book and say what is to be done. {npc} has already found the book and is reading it very carefully, with one finger. {gn_room} are waiting for someone to tell them whose grandfather to dust.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Hold out your hand for the book

effects.log: {npc} looks up, marks {his} place, and closes it. "Shall we say behind the well?" {he} says, in the nicest possible way.

choices.text: Ask {npc} which grandfather you should start with

effects.log: {He} tells you. You start. It is a very peaceful way to lose an argument.

choices.text: Pick up a cloth, and start with the one nobody has dusted

effects.log: The old man has been waiting about two hundred years, by the look of the tablet. You find out the name and say it aloud. It seems only polite.

events.text: A Keeper has come to ask, gently, who is the head of your household. This has to go in the city's book. It is only a formality, the Keeper says, but those listed as the head are held to answer for the rest. The last head of this house was the merchant. The Keeper does not mention how that ended. {npc} has straightened {his} robe. {gn_room} seem to have become very interested in the floor.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Say "I am", before {npc} can

effects.log: "Thank you," says the Keeper. {npc} also says thank you, later, and rather more thoroughly, behind the well.

choices.text: Say {npc}'s name

effects.log: {npc} gives you a small nod, as between two people who now understand how this will work. The Keeper writes it down.

choices.text: Say that the merchant is still the head of the house

effects.log: There is a pause. The Keeper smiles for the first time, and writes that down. It is, you are told afterwards, entirely correct.

events.text: In a city with no one in it, the living find one another in small quiet groups, like people on a very long boat. {gn_clique} meets on a certain step at dusk. They have asked you, by leaving a space on the step, and by not looking at it. There is another, grander group who have taken over the old governor's hall, and have started setting a place for the governor.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Sit down in the space on the step

effects.log: Nobody says anything for an hour. It is the most welcome you have ever been made to feel.

choices.text: Go up to the governor's hall

effects.log: They look you over, kindly, and then set a place for you just below the governor. It is a very cold seat.

choices.text: Light a fire in your dead merchant's kitchen, and leave the door open

effects.log: You would not have thought anything could look so bright. By midwinter there are nine of you in there, all pretending they just happened to be passing.

choices.text: Walk the streets alone at dusk

effects.log: You walk the streets alone. After some time you find the streets have begun to expect you.

events.text: There is a difficulty about the Festival of Late Visitors. Every group in the School will walk its own procession, and {gn_clique} has asked, in writing, whether you would care to carry the third lantern. The strongest procession has asked nobody at all, and is simply going to happen, through everyone. The Keepers have let it be known that they are looking forward to it very much.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Carry the third lantern for {gn_clique}

effects.log: It is a slow, solemn, ridiculous business. You trip over a dead man's step. You have not been so happy in a long time.

choices.text: Walk with the strongest, and try not to be walked over

effects.log: You keep your feet. It is harder than most of the fighting you have done. They notice, without seeming to.

choices.text: Start a procession of your own, in the other direction

effects.log: Nobody has ever gone the other way. All the processions meet in the Fish Market, in dead silence, and stand there. The Keepers talk of it for years.

choices.text: Stay in and write to the people on the merchant's tablets

effects.log: You write them all a short polite note, and you burn them in the correct way. It feels like the first sensible thing you have done here.

events.text: Your rival has arrived in the ghost city. You should have known. They walk down the middle of the Street of Coffin-Makers with {gn_rival_clique} walking behind them in step, and they raise their lantern to you very slightly as they pass. You have never seen them so well-mannered. It is, by a long way, the most alarming thing about them.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Raise your lantern, and fall in behind them

effects.log: You fall in. "How kind," your rival says, without turning. You have the odd feeling of having walked into an old story, at the wrong end.

choices.text: Go and sit with {gn_clique}, where they can see you

effects.log: You sit down on the step. Your rival inclines their head, and you incline yours. It is a declaration of war, of the very best quality.

choices.text: Set your own procession across their path

effects.log: Neither procession stops, or speeds up, or says a word. It takes all night. Nobody who was there ever forgets it.

choices.text: Bow and go on your way, alone

effects.log: You bow. They bow. You go on your way alone. Behind you, somebody quietly starts to laugh.

events.text: There is a paper boat on your step this morning. There was one yesterday, and the day before. It has your name written on its sail, in the elegant hand they use for tablets, and it is pointing at the river. {npc} is sitting on the wall across the street with paper in {his} lap, folding, and wishes you a very good morning. The School has one law, and {he} knows it as well as you do.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Wish {him} good morning, and collect the boats

effects.log: You put them on a shelf, each one, with the dates. You will have quite a collection. So will {he} have something to answer for.

choices.text: Ask the Keepers for a hearing in the empty square

effects.log: A hearing is what they call it. There is no talking. {npc} folds up {his} paper, and looks delighted to have been asked.

choices.text: Carry the boats to a Keeper in a basket

effects.log: The Keeper admires the folding very much. Then {npc} is asked, with great courtesy, to spend a season dusting the Street of Coffin-Makers, all of it.

choices.text: Go across the street and add {him} to the city

effects.log: You put down your lantern. It is the first time you have been quite sure what you were doing. Somebody down the street begins, unhurriedly, to run.

events.text: Someone has been having a word with the household. The merchant's tablets have all been turned to the wall, and the rice has been set out on the wrong days. A Keeper has stopped by to mention, very kindly, that the household is displeased, and that you have been so careful up to now. {npc} passes you in the street and asks how the household is keeping.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Turn each one back, and apologise to them

effects.log: It takes you a week. You are very thorough. By the end of it, you have the strangest impression that the household is on your side.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to meet you in the empty square

effects.log: "I thought you might," says {npc}, and {he} bows. In this place, that is about as angry as anyone ever gets.

choices.text: Show the Keeper the wax from {his} candle on the shelf

effects.log: The Keeper looks at the wax for a long time. "How careless," the Keeper says, and {npc}, the next day, has a very unpleasant visit from {his} own ancestors, in the form of paperwork.

choices.text: Wait for {him} by the well at midnight, and end it

effects.log: There is one law. You find you have been standing by the well for quite a while, and that you have made up your mind.

events.text: They have given out the winter walk, and {npc} is to walk behind you. It is an old exercise. You walk the dark city together with one lantern, unlit, and you try to feel where the other is. All you have to do is not turn round. {He} has been, for six nights now, standing very slightly closer than {he} was the night before. {He} has not touched you. {He} just breathes, politely.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Do not turn round

effects.log: You do not turn round. It is the longest winter of your life, and you are extremely good at it by the end. So is {he}.

choices.text: Turn round and offer {him} the square

effects.log: You turn. {npc} is much closer than you thought. {He} looks pleased. "At last," {he} says. "I was getting so tired."

choices.text: Tell the Keeper exactly how close

effects.log: You give the distance in fingers. The Keeper nods and arranges for someone else to walk behind {npc}, for the rest of the winter. You hear {him} start to walk faster.

choices.text: Turn round and do not stop

effects.log: You turn round and you do not stop, and the lantern goes rolling away down the street. It seems very loud.

events.text: On the last night of the last year, every student left in the School lights their lantern for the first time. Then you all go walking into the dark city, and each of you does what you can to put out the others, by any art you have, but no one may be added to the city. The last lantern lit is the {sda_title}, of {gn_gen}. The Keepers have brought out their good chairs.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Light your lantern and walk in

effects.log: It is a small warm light. You had forgotten what colour they were. You shield it with your hand, and you go in.

choices.text: Light it, hang it on the gate, and sit down beside it

effects.log: You sit down beside it and wait for the morning. Nobody bothers you. It burns all night, in fact, but it does not count, and the Keepers bow to you anyway.

events.text: The day before the last walk, you go around the merchant's house and say goodbye to the family, tablet by tablet. {gn_room} have the same idea. You meet them on the stairs with a cloth. In four years, you have got quite fond of the grandfather. Tomorrow night the School will decide who is the {sda_title}, and you could, you suppose, simply stay here and finish the dusting.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Finish the dusting, then go and win it

effects.log: You finish it. You do the corners. Then you go and pick up a lantern, feeling that you have a family behind you, whoever they are.

choices.text: Stay in, and have dinner with the family

effects.log: You set the table for all of them and for yourself. It is a very good dinner. Far away, in the dark, the lanterns are going out.

events.text: At the gate with no guards, a Keeper is sitting on a stool and takes your lantern from you and writes something in a book. "Those of the {sda_ladder} would be glad of you," the Keeper says. "They walk for the sect now. Or you may have those who would follow you. Or there is the world, I believe. I have heard it is very noisy." The Keeper looks up. "We should so like you to come back, in due course."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Walk with the {sda_ladder}

effects.log: They make room, without looking round. You fall into step. You find you know exactly how fast they are going.
