choices.text: Turn and look for those who would follow you

effects.log: They are behind you, closer than you thought, very quietly. You should have expected that. It was you who taught them.

choices.text: Go out into the noise

effects.log: You thank the Keeper for everything. You go out. It is very loud, and the sun is on everything, and you stand there for a while, and it is wonderful.

events.text: You go back to the merchant's house one last time. You turn the tablets to face the door, so that they can see you off. On the kitchen table, somebody has left a list in that elegant hand. It has your name and a choice of three: the {sda_ladder} in their grey, the names of those who would go with you, and a small drawing of a road. At the bottom it says, "No hurry."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Choose the grey

effects.log: You fold the list up into a boat, and carry it with you to the {sda_ladder}. They are very pleased about the folding.

choices.text: Go and wake the ones on the list

effects.log: They were not asleep. They come as they are, with one good lantern between you all.

choices.text: Choose the road

effects.log: You leave the note on the table for the next one, with the road circled. It seems only fair.

events.text: You are in a crowded street, at noon, when you see a tiny paper boat on a stall among the dumplings, and then another one on the sill of the tailor's, and then you stop, because {npc} is standing just behind your left shoulder and has been, you suspect, for a little while. "How do you do," {he} says quietly. "It is such a long time. There are no Keepers here, you know. I have checked."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Say good afternoon, and walk with {him} out of town

effects.log: You walk out of town together, in step, talking of the weather. You could not tell you when you last enjoyed a conversation so much.

choices.text: Tell {him} one of you is going back to the city today

effects.log: "How thoughtful," says {npc}, and {he} is entirely sincere. You go somewhere quieter, and you take off your coat.

choices.text: Pick up the boat and put it in the gutter, with the rain

effects.log: You both watch it go off along the gutter and round the corner. Neither of you says anything for a time. {He} bows lower than you have ever seen.

choices.text: Buy {him} a dumpling and leave

effects.log: You pay for a dumpling, and you put it in {his} hand, and you leave. It will take {him} some time to decide what you meant. You will have that long.

events.text: A letter from {npc}, the first in years, in that very beautiful hand. {He} hopes you are well. {He} would be most obliged if you could spare an evening, at the crossroads shrine, for a small matter left unfinished in the School. {He} mentions the date, and asks after your health again. There is no threat in it from beginning to end, and you read it four times.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Go to the crossroads, on the day, on time

effects.log: You are both on time, of course. You have both brought your own lamp, and you put them down an equal distance from the shrine.

choices.text: Go early, and end it there

effects.log: {npc} is earlier. {He} rises and bows, and neither of you says it, but you both see you will not need two lamps going home.

choices.text: Write back, a very long, very kind letter

effects.log: It takes you a month. When you are done you have forgiven {him}, rather to your surprise. {His} reply is one line. You keep it.

choices.text: Decline, with thanks

effects.log: You decline with thanks. {He} thanks you for your thanks. You are sure {he} will write again.

events.text: {npc}, the Keeper who teaches your year, takes you all out on the first night to a street of empty houses and asks you to tell {him} who lived in each. You protest that nobody could know. {He} looks surprised. "They are all still there," {he} says. "It is very rude not to ask." So you go in, by yourself, and sit down in somebody's kitchen. After some time, you begin to get an idea.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Write the name down, and keep it

effects.log: {npc} checks it in {his} book and looks at you with deep pleasure. "That is one," {he} says. "We shall want you to look after that name now. You are the only one who knows."

choices.text: Say you do not know, but you tidied up a bit

effects.log: {npc} laughs, a small dry sound like a page turning. "Then I expect they know you," {he} says.

choices.text: Say it is an empty house, and you are cold

effects.log: {npc} nods, kindly, and goes on to the next student. As you pass the door, you have the feeling of someone turning away.

events.text: The art of the Ashen Veil, {npc} tells you, is not a matter of hiding. It is a matter of being so well-behaved that nobody remembers you were there. {He} has you practise by walking through the market in the next town and buying a turnip, and returning without the stallholder being able to say whether you came. {He} has been standing next to you for the whole of this explanation, it seems.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Go and buy a name along with the turnip

effects.log: You come back with the turnip, and with the stallholder's dead mother's name, told to you without noticing. {npc} is enormously impressed. Another for the city.

choices.text: Go and buy a turnip

effects.log: You buy a turnip. The stallholder looks straight through you and asks if you have seen a customer. {npc} bows slightly when you get back.

choices.text: Say you would rather be remembered, thank you

effects.log: {npc} tilts {his} head. "Most people do," {he} says. "Up to a point." You get the turnip thrown at you, gently, by nobody you can see.

events.text: It is the day of the Ash Register. {npc} shows your year the great book of everyone the city has ever taken in, in hundreds of hands, and tells you that it is nearly full. "When it is full," {he} says, "we will start another book." You ask who is at the end. {He} turns the page around, and there are the names of the current students, in pencil, with a small polite question mark after each.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Ask if you may read the whole book

effects.log: It takes you all the winter. {npc} brings you tea. You are the only one in forty years who has asked, and you come out with a great many names, and a cold.

choices.text: Borrow {his} pencil and rub out your question mark

effects.log: {npc} watches, and takes back the pencil. {He} seems pleased. "We do admire confidence," {he} says. {He} writes it back in afterwards, very faintly.

choices.text: Close the book

effects.log: You close it, gently, and step back. It is not your book. {npc} does not reopen it while you are there.

events.text: {npc} has asked you to dinner in the last winter, at {his} own house, which has a roof, and a table set for nine. You and {he} are the only ones eating. {He} says there is a vow that the sect keeps, if you should care to take it on, and you may say it here, in front of the family. "They are very discreet," {he} says. "But it is a great deal to carry. There is no shame in merely finishing the soup."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Stand up, and swear it to the table

effects.log: You say it to all nine places. {npc} listens gravely, and then {he} and all the empty chairs seem to relax, slightly. You finish the soup.

choices.text: Ask whose places these are, and learn them

effects.log: {He} tells you, one by one, over the soup. They are all people {he} has outlived. You offer to look after the list. {He} cannot speak for a moment.

choices.text: Finish the soup

effects.log: It is excellent soup. {npc} seems perfectly content. So, as far as you can tell, does everyone else.

events.text: In the spring of your last year {npc} takes you to the city wall at dawn and gives you the last thing: how to go out. "Everyone here wants to know how to come in," {he} says. "It is quite easy. Nobody ever asks me how to leave." It is a very short lesson. You could swear it is mostly about noticing things, like a bird or a smell of bread. There is a vow you might take as well, {he} adds, if you feel the need of one.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Swear your vow, there on the wall

effects.log: The sun comes up while you are saying it. {npc} takes it down in {his} book, and then, with a slight frown, in ink.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} never left

effects.log: "Oh," says {npc}. "I did. Twice. It was lovely." {He} looks out at the road for a long time. "They do need someone to keep the book." You take a few names off {his} hands.

choices.text: Stand and notice things, for as long as {he} will let you

effects.log: There is a bird. There is a smell of bread, from a very long way off. You stand there till noon, and {he} stands with you.

events.text: It is the merchant's birthday. You worked it out from the household book, and so did {npc}, and neither of you told the other. You both come down at dusk, each with a very small cake, and meet in front of the tablet. There is a long pause. {He} says, "The merchant would have liked a bigger one." You have never heard {him} make a joke before. You are not entirely sure that this is one.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Light a candle and have the cakes together

effects.log: You sing to the tablet, very quietly and badly. The whole street seems to listen. It is the nicest evening of the year.

choices.text: Leave your cake, bow, and go up

effects.log: You leave it and go. Later you hear {npc} in the kitchen, talking to the merchant about {his} day, and you lie awake and do not join in.

events.text: There is a thing the older students do. You go up on the roof of the Drum Tower on a clear night in autumn, and lie on your backs, and {npc} tells you which of the lights in the valley are the living towns. There are not many. They look warm and very busy. {He} has been coming up here for two years, it turns out, and has given them all names. One of them {he} thinks must be {his} mother's.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you about that one

effects.log: You lie there until the light goes out in that town. {npc} waits a little longer, then gets up, and neither of you says anything on the way down.

choices.text: Pick out your own and keep it to yourself

effects.log: You pick one out. It is not the right one, you are fairly sure. You look at it anyway. {npc} goes on naming them without you.

events.text: A dog has come into the city. No one knows how. It is a stupid, cheerful yellow dog, and it goes barking down the Street of Coffin-Makers, and every student in the School comes out to stare. The Keepers are looking pained. {npc} has got down on {his} knees in the road, in {his} grey robes, and the dog is licking {his} whole face, and {he} seems to be crying, though {he} would never say so.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Get down there and help

effects.log: It licks you as well. It is the loudest thing that has happened here in a hundred years. You name it Merchant.

choices.text: Go and get the Keeper a chair

effects.log: You make yourself useful. You feel a very long way off, somehow. The dog stays on, and everyone but you seems to know its name.

events.text: You find {npc} sitting in the kitchen of your house when you come in. {He} is one of the great Keepers, the white-chair kind, and {he} rose to bow to you before you had quite seen {him}, which you find upsetting. {He} has been going through your lists of names and {he} is very impressed. "It would be a kindness to an old person," {he} says, "if you were to come and help, after. There is so much to keep."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Say it would be an honour

effects.log: It will be. It also means that someone will always know where you are. {npc} seems to think that is the nice part.

choices.text: Say you could not possibly impose

effects.log: It is the right form of words. {npc} bows, and thanks you for your consideration. {He} is gone when you turn round. {He} leaves your list slightly straighter.

events.text: At the Festival of Late Visitors, someone walks for some time in step behind you, and when you stop, it is {npc}. "I knew your grandmother," {he} says. You did not know that anyone here knew you had one. "A difficult woman, and a good one. I would like to take an interest in you. People in the white-chair hall do listen to me, mostly out of fear that I will remember something."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Tell {him} you would be glad of it

effects.log: {He} tells you a story about your grandmother that you will never, ever repeat. It is the start of something.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} remembers about you

effects.log: {He} tells you. You thank {him} and say you will manage alone, thanks. {npc} smiles and goes on walking, a little behind you, for some time.

events.text: {npc} has come from the Grey Procession to walk the School's third-years, and at the end {he} stops you, very politely, and gives you a slip of paper with a name on it. "That is someone important, who has not died yet," {he} says. "When {he} does, a certain position will open in the white-chair hall. I should like you to be standing nearby. If you agree, I shall begin to mention you."
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Agree

effects.log: You keep the slip. {npc} begins to mention you. You begin to find that people stand up, slightly, when you come into a room.

choices.text: Hand back the slip

effects.log: You hand it back, bowing. "Very wise," says {npc}. "Or perhaps not. We shall have plenty of time to find out."

events.text: You have kept names for the city, and the city has been very patient. A polite person brings you a paper boat with a note in it. Would you be so kind as to come and look after them yourself? It would only be for a few years. Or the Keepers would accept {sda_cost} taels for someone else's trouble, or a small errand on behalf of the dead. {sda_teacher} sends regards. There is no hurry, the note adds. There never is.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Send the silver: {sda_cost} taels, with thanks

effects.log: You send it, with a very long note, and they send a very long note of thanks for the note. You are free of it. You miss the names, a little.

choices.text: Run the errand

effects.log: It is a very quiet errand. You will not tell anybody about it. Nobody, as it turns out, will be in a position to ask.

choices.text: Write back, with great regret, no

effects.log: They reply, with great regret, that they understand completely. Somebody starts walking a little behind you, some days. You never quite catch them.

events.text: There is someone sitting on your step, in grey, who has clearly been there all night and has not minded at all. "One of the names you kept has come loose," they say. "It happens. It has been asking after you. It would be such a help if you could see to it. Or there is the fee, {sda_cost} taels, and the Keepers will see to it themselves." They offer you a very small, very beautiful, very old cake.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Eat the cake, and pay the fee

effects.log: You pay. It is quite a good cake, considering. You do not ask what became of the name. You think of it, some nights, anyway.

choices.text: Go and see to it yourself

effects.log: You go. You will say this much: it was a long way, and the person was very glad to see you, and you should not have gone alone.

choices.text: Tell them the name can go and ask someone else

effects.log: They look at you with great gentleness. "It will," they say. "That is what we were afraid of." They go off, and someone new starts asking for you by name.

events.text: You have started hearing your name in empty rooms. It is nothing, it is very polite. It is only the Register, a note explains, in that lovely hand: your pencil question mark has gone a little dark, and the Keepers would be so glad to have it seen to. {sda_cost} taels will buy a rubber, as it were. Or there is someone who needs a thing brought to them, in the city, tonight. {sda_teacher} sends, again, regards.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Buy the rubber: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: It is the first thing you ever bought with no goods to show for it. The rooms go quiet. You had no idea how loud they had been.

choices.text: Bring the thing

effects.log: You bring it. You do not look inside. You are shown out, very courteously, by something that is not quite a person.

choices.text: Write your own name in the Register, in ink, and send it

effects.log: You send them your name in ink, with no question mark. It seems very funny, for about a week. Someone is sent to look into it.

events.text: The tailor says there was someone in asking after you. Very polite, very grey. The face will not quite come back to the tailor. You find {npc} at the end of the street, buying a turnip, and it takes you a moment to see {him} even though you are looking straight at {him}. "I do beg your pardon," {he} says. "I forget I do that, now." You have not seen {him} in years.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Ask {him} home to dinner

effects.log: You lay an extra place. Then you lay a few more, and you both laugh, and then {he} tells you who they are for.

choices.text: Bow, and let {him} go back to being unnoticed

effects.log: {He} bows. You blink. You are alone in the street with a faint smell of turnip, and you are not sure {he} was ever there.

events.text: A yellow dog comes to your door, very old, and then {npc}, a little older, walking slowly so as not to get ahead of it. "This is Merchant," {he} says. "The grandson, I mean, I think. This one has been wanting to see you." The dog falls asleep on your foot. It is a hot, loud, ordinary afternoon, and {npc} sits down on the step and looks at the street with great attention, as if somebody had just made it.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Sit down too, and bring out something to drink

effects.log: You sit till evening. You tell {him} what you have been doing, and {he} listens and asks after the household, one by one, by name.

choices.text: Tell {him} you have a great deal to do today

effects.log: It is true. {npc} nods, and gets up, slowly, and the dog does too. You wish later that you had looked up.

events.text: {npc} has written to tell you {he} has got your merchant's house now. {He} has put on a second roof. {He} has dusted the grandfather, and has told the tablet all about you. {He} would be delighted if you came back to see it, in due course, and {he} has underlined "in due course" very lightly in pencil. You think that it may be a joke. It is exactly the sort of thing that would be, and also not be.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Write back and tell {him} what you have become

effects.log: You write it all down, the whole of it, more than you have told anyone. Then you add: "Tell Grandfather I am keeping well." It is a good letter.

choices.text: Write back two polite lines

effects.log: They are two very correct lines. They could have been written by anybody. You see that, as you seal it, and you send it anyway.

events.text: {npc} comes in very quietly and takes a chair, and has apparently been in it for some time. {He} has heard, in the white-chair hall, that there is some question of who is to sit in the seat after you. {He} and those from the dead merchant's house would so like to be useful. {He} only needs to know which of the children you would like them to look after, or whether you would rather {he} left it all alone.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Name {sda_side}

effects.log: "So thoughtful," says {npc}, and takes out {his} little book. Somehow, the room has got colder. {sda_side} is very well looked after from now on.

choices.text: Name the child nobody looks after

effects.log: {npc} looks up. It is the first time you have seen {him} surprised. "How kind," {he} says, and you can see {he} means it.

choices.text: Thank {him}, and ask {him} to leave it all alone

effects.log: {He} bows. {He} is a good guest, and goes. Nothing is left in the room, not a mark, not a chill. You find that you are rather sorry.

events.text: A paper boat on the desk, among the reports. It has two names on its sail, an elder child's and {sda_side}'s, and a small question mark in pencil. It is {npc}'s folding, you would know it anywhere. {He} is waiting at the door, and asks after your health. It seems the Keepers have begun to hold a small friendly book on which of the children they will have the honour of receiving first.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Rub out everything on the sail but {sda_side}

effects.log: {npc} takes it back, and admires it. "Then we shall see that the other name is well attended," {he} says. {He} says it very gently.

choices.text: Write in the name nobody has thought of

effects.log: You write it. {npc} reads it twice. "What a very great deal of trouble," {he} says happily, and goes off to tell no one.

choices.text: Put the boat on the fire

effects.log: It burns with a small clean flame. You both watch. "Well," says {npc}. "There will be others. But I will tell them you said so."

events.text: A very polite letter tells you that {sda_teacher} has moved house. It gives the new address, which is a street in the ghost city you remember well. {sda_teacher} is settling in very nicely, it says, and sends regards, and hopes you are still keeping the names. Would you consider dropping by, in due course? There is a place laid. You notice that the handwriting on the letter is the same as it has always been.
events.arc: The School of the Unlit Lantern

choices.text: Write back with all the names you still remember

effects.log: It is quite a long list. It is all of them, in fact, every one. You had not known that. You sign it, and thank {sda_teacher} for the soup.

choices.text: Light a lantern at your gate, tonight, and every year

effects.log: You light it, and leave it burning. Your household thinks you have become sentimental. You let them think so.

events.text: A woman with a purser's ring of keys is sitting on your fence, eating your neighbour's plums. "The River School," she says. "Four years, on the barges, a new reach each year, all seven of the old outfits teaching and none of them in charge. You pay when you can. Everyone does. In the end." She flicks away a stone. "There is a landing at the bend, the day after tomorrow. We do not wait, but we do come back."

choices.text: Be at the landing

effects.log: You are there before dawn. She looks at you and sighs: "Keen. That goes on your account." You sign on a wet plank.

choices.text: Say you do not like the sound of the interest

effects.log: "Nobody does," she says, without offence, and hops down, and takes the rest of the plums. "That is the first useful thing you have learned."

events.text: They catch you at something, not quite legal, not quite stupid. It is not the magistrate who has seen it. It is a fat ferryman with one eyebrow, who has followed you for two streets to tell you that you did it very badly. "You have got hands," he says. "Nobody has told you what they are for. There is a school. It takes people like you, and it does not ask what they are running from. It only asks what you can pay."

choices.text: Ask when the boat goes

effects.log: "When it goes," he says, and he laughs till he has to sit down. The boat goes that night. You are on it.

choices.text: Tell him you will keep doing it badly, on your own

effects.log: "You will," he says, sadly, and he pats your shoulder and takes your purse. He gives it back at the corner. You did not notice either time.

events.text: Word has come down the water: the Long Bend chapter wants you. They have had your name from someone at the stronghold, or the Pavilion, or the Valley, nobody will say which, and now you are on the purser's list with a little tick by it. An old pole-man brings you the terms. Four years of teaching, from all seven of the old outfits. No one owns the barges. There is, he mentions, a lot of small print.

choices.text: Sign, and read the small print on the way

effects.log: You read it on the way. You are the first person he has ever seen do that. He is not sure he approves.

choices.text: Tell him you will do without the small print and the school

effects.log: He shrugs and poles off downstream. It is a very wide river. There is a lot of it, and it is all going somewhere without you.

events.text: You are given the stern of the third barge, with {npc}, {gn_room}, and everything the barge does not want. There is one dry corner, the size of a large dog. It is the only dry corner on the river. {npc} is sitting in it with {his} boots off, and is looking at you with the mild friendly interest of a person who has already priced you. The barge is moving. The truce holds on the water, but the truce only covers blades.

choices.text: Tip {him} out of it

effects.log: You take {him} by the belt. {npc} grins. There is no blade in it, so the truce has nothing to say, and the barge's crew gather to watch.

choices.text: Offer {him} a fair rent to share

effects.log: {npc} is delighted. You work out terms. You are in debt to a person you have known for an hour, and it is all very friendly.

choices.text: Sit on the wet side, and start learning the river

effects.log: You get thoroughly soaked. By the end of the week, you can tell the depth by the sound. {npc} starts to look interested.

events.text: Every stern on every barge has somebody who deals with the purser for the rest, and takes a small cut for it. {npc} has been telling {gn_room} that it is {him}. Nobody can remember agreeing to it. The first week's bill is about to come round. It will be much too high, and there will be a person who has to go up the plank and argue, and that person will be the one everyone owes.

choices.text: Get to the purser first, with your own numbers

effects.log: You get there first. The purser looks at your sums, and then at you. "Who taught you to count like a thief?" comes the approving question. {npc} is waiting back at the stern with {his} sleeves rolled up.

choices.text: Let {npc} go up the plank, and pay the cut

effects.log: It is a good cut for {him}, and a fair deal for you, and you get to watch how it is done. You do watch.

choices.text: Go up with your own bill and pay for yourself only

effects.log: The purser laughs out loud. So does everyone. You are not anyone's, and they will all be pleased to explain what that costs.

events.text: It is a knot game, the first night. It is always a knot game. It is played on an upturned tub at the stern, for prizes that begin as jokes and end as the dry corner, the good rope, who bails, who eats first. {npc} is running it. {He} is, you notice, very good, and {gn_room} are very bad, and {he} hands you the rope with a very big smile. Somebody on the next barge shouts for silence.

choices.text: Catch {him} using a trick rope and say so with a straight face

effects.log: {npc} looks at the rope you have pulled apart, and then at you. "Well," {he} says, "that leaves only the old way, then." {He} stands up.

choices.text: Lose carefully, and let {him} see you did it

effects.log: You lose just enough. {npc} winks. You are on {his} side of the tub for the rest of the year, and you learn a good deal about rope.

choices.text: Say you do not play, and go and watch the banks

effects.log: You watch the banks go by. The moon is up. Behind you someone loses a boot. You have no debts tonight, and that is rare here.

events.text: Second year, and the barges have sorted themselves out, along the lines of who owes whom. {gn_clique} have been buying up small debts of people they like. They have bought one of yours. It was very nicely done, and there is a note saying so. Up on the lead barge, the strongest crew owes nobody, and everyone owes them. And you could always keep your own books, if you are good enough.

choices.text: Go and thank {gn_clique}, and join

effects.log: You find them on the slack side, eating eels, and you sit down. You now owe people who like you, and it makes a real difference.

choices.text: Swim to the lead barge and ask for work

effects.log: They haul you up, dripping. "What can you do?" You show them. A fat girl with a gaff looks at you, and says you can stay until you are a bother.

choices.text: Start buying up debts yourself

effects.log: You begin with the ones nobody wants. By spring you own a bit of everyone on your barge. They elect you something, out of self-defence.

choices.text: Pay off the note, and keep your own books

effects.log: You pay off the note with your last silver. "No one is your friend out here if you owe no one," the eel-sellers tell you. You will find out.

events.text: The Black Wind's young sit with the Black Wind's, the Valley's with the Valley's, and the Pavilion's just seem to be everywhere, and you cannot quite remember seeing them come in. But on the river, it is the crews that count, and crews cut across all of that. {gn_clique} has a poison girl, two bandits and a pickpocket, and they are looking for someone who can steer. So is everyone, it seems.

choices.text: Steer for {gn_clique}

effects.log: You take the long pole. They are very bad people, and the best crew you have ever been in. You have stopped worrying about which you mean.

choices.text: Go with the crew everyone is afraid of

effects.log: You make yourself useful to them, and they are not grateful. But nobody bothers you at the landing any more.

choices.text: Get your stern to crew together

effects.log: Four people and a tub. It should not float. It does, by spite. The others stop laughing at the Bend, where you pass them.

choices.text: Hire out by the day to whoever is paying

effects.log: You work for all of them. You learn all their tricks. None of them invite you to the eels.

events.text: You cannot believe it. Your rival is on the river too, in somebody else's boots, with {gn_rival_clique} around them, holding court on a raft they appear to have stolen. They catch sight of you across the water, and stand up, and bow extravagantly, and fall in. Their crew fishes them out. When they have stopped coughing, they shout that there is a place for you, at very reasonable rates.

choices.text: Pole over and take the place

effects.log: You go. "I knew you were broke," your rival says, wringing out a sleeve. It turns out to be easier to hate someone when you are sharing the eels.

choices.text: Shout back a rude number, and go to {gn_clique}

effects.log: You shout it clear across the reach. The whole river laughs. You sit down with {gn_clique}, and your rival shouts a ruder one.

choices.text: Tell them you will have that raft by spring

effects.log: You build your crew up for just that purpose. You have it by midwinter, as it happens. It is a very bad raft.

choices.text: Pretend you did not hear

effects.log: You keep your eyes on the bank. The shouting goes on for a good while. You work out afterwards that it was quite well-informed.

events.text: A piece of paper is going round the barges. It is your debt, or a piece of it, and {npc} has bought it, at a very good price. {He} comes along the plank to show you. It says that you owe {him} a day's work a week, and there is a little line about what you do on that day, in {his} handwriting. {He} is quite within {his} rights. The truce holds on the water, and {he} is very careful never to take you ashore.

choices.text: Do the work, and read everything {he} signs

effects.log: You do it, all of it. And you read everything that crosses {his} table, because {he} has made you carry it. You are going to enjoy this, eventually.

choices.text: Tell {him} there is a sandbar at the next bend

effects.log: A sandbar is not the water. Everyone on the barge knows it. {npc} smiles and asks if you would prefer the morning.

choices.text: Take the paper up to the purser and dispute it

effects.log: You find three mistakes in it, and the purser finds a fourth. {npc} has to pay a fee, and {he} tips {his} hat to you, in a way you will think about later.

choices.text: Draw a blade on {him}, on the water

effects.log: Everyone on the barge goes very quiet. Nobody draws on the water. There are seven sects' children here, and that is the only reason any of them have ever slept.

events.text: Something has happened to the third barge's rope, and somebody has told the Bargemaster it was you. Then something happens to your boots, and then to your bed. There is never any blade in it, you must admit, and it is really very imaginative. {npc} leans on the rail and says it is a shame how bad your luck has been this year. {He} is offering to sell you some insurance.

choices.text: Buy the insurance, and keep the receipt

effects.log: You buy it. Your luck improves at once. You keep all the receipts in a dry bag, and you have a very good memory for what they will be worth.

choices.text: Pay {him} a visit on the next sandbar

effects.log: You send a formal note. {npc} sends back a time. {He} also sends a price list for a seat on the bank, and half the barge buys one.

choices.text: Bring the Bargemaster the cut end of the rope

effects.log: You show exactly whose knife made it. The Bargemaster looks from one of you to the other, and then charges you both, on principle. {He} gets the bigger bill, though.

choices.text: Get {him} alone at the rail in the dark, with a blade

effects.log: It is a long way down, and very dark. You are not on a sandbar. You have stopped caring about that.

events.text: They have started a song about you. You find out when a pole-boy asks you, with some embarrassment, how you are feeling. {npc} wrote it. It goes round the seven outfits, a new verse a week, and in every verse you do not last the year. The last verse is left blank, {he} tells you in a friendly way, and {he} is really quite looking forward to filling it in.

choices.text: Learn every verse, and work on what they mock

effects.log: You train on the worst verse first. It is the best thing that could have happened to you. You will also want a word with the singer, later.

choices.text: Make it a bout on the sandbar, in front of the singers

effects.log: Half the river turns up. Some of them bring lunch. {npc} stretches, and gives you a nod. {He} needs a good last verse.

choices.text: Tell the purser the song has not paid its dues

effects.log: It has not, as it turns out. The River charges for everything. The purser takes a very close interest, and {npc} is suddenly short of funds and in a rather different mood.

choices.text: Finish the last verse tonight with a blade, truce or no truce

effects.log: There is a blank verse with your name on it, and an easier way to fill it, you think, and you take your knife out.

events.text: The last race runs through the Three Sisters Gorge in the flood. All the crews, all the barges, and everything goes, short of killing, with the Bargemasters watching from the cliffs, and half the Greenwood and the Water Gang down on the banks come to watch. The one who is on their feet at the bottom landing is the {sda_title} of {gn_gen}. The water is the colour of tea and it is going very fast.

choices.text: Take the long pole and go

effects.log: You spit on your hands. The first Sister is already coming up, and she looks bigger than you remember.

choices.text: Sit it out on the bank, and sell tea

effects.log: You find a dry rock and a kettle. You study the crews carefully, and the crowd pays well. Some people are going to be sorry they laughed.

events.text: The night before the gorge, {gn_room} are sitting at the stern, and somebody has stolen a whole duck. You have all been on this water for four years, and nobody has said anything nice to anyone in all that time, and it seems a bit late to start. The purser comes by with her keys, and tells each of you what you owe, so that you will know what you are playing for.

choices.text: Say you will pay it all off with the {sda_title}'s purse

effects.log: {gn_room} laugh so hard that one of them drops the duck. You pick it up. You are going to do it, though.

choices.text: Say the crown can go hang, and pass the duck

effects.log: It is a very good duck. It is a very good night. In the morning, you wave them off from the landing, and you mean it.

events.text: The last landing. The purser reads your account to you, with interest, and has you put your thumb on it. "Open," she says, and shuts the book. Up the bank there is a man from the Greenwood looking for fighters. Down by the willows there is someone who was not there a moment ago, from the Hushed Lantern, looking for something else. Your crew are hanging about with their bags, pretending they have nowhere to go.

choices.text: Go up the bank to the {sda_ladder}

effects.log: He looks you over. "Toll-roads," he says. "Tolls we understand." You have a horse by nightfall, and you owe him for it.

choices.text: Go down to the willows, to the {sda_ladder2}

effects.log: Nobody is at the willows when you get there. There is a small note, addressed to you, in your own handwriting. You follow it.

choices.text: Whistle to your crew

effects.log: They pick up their bags, complaining bitterly. They have no idea why they are following you. They have, however, read your account.

choices.text: Walk along the bank, on your own

effects.log: Nobody looks up. A river is a very good place to have come from. You whistle.

events.text: You have stepped off the plank before you notice that it is the last time. The barge is already moving out, on to a new reach, with new people, and someone you do not know is sitting in the dry corner. On the landing there are two tables with recruiters, and a stack of crates, and {gn_room}, who ask what you are planning to do. You realise it is the first time in four years that nobody has charged you for an answer.

choices.text: Go to the {sda_ladder}'s table

effects.log: You sign, and you read the small print. The recruiter is annoyed. It is a good sign.

choices.text: Go to the table with nobody sitting at it

effects.log: You sit down on the {sda_ladder2}'s side. After a while, you notice someone has been across from you for quite some time.

choices.text: Tell them all you have an idea

effects.log: They groan. They know your ideas. They come along anyway, carrying the crates.

choices.text: Say you are going to go and find out

effects.log: They say they thought so. Someone gives you the duck's wishbone, and you find it in your sleeve a week later.

events.text: You are crossing a little bridge, in a town far from any water you know, when {npc} stops you with a piece of paper. It is your old debt, the very same piece, gone soft along the folds, and {he} has been charging interest on it for all this time. {He} shows you the sum. It is very funny. {He} is laughing. "We are ashore now," {he} says, and there is nothing funny about that at all.

choices.text: Offer to settle it the shore's way

effects.log: You put down your bag. {npc} folds the paper away carefully, in case. It is a good bridge for it.

choices.text: Say you will close the account for good

effects.log: The bridge is empty. {npc} stops laughing and looks at you, with interest, and without much surprise.

choices.text: Take the paper, and drop it in the stream

effects.log: You both lean over the rail to watch it go. {npc} sighs. "That was worth a lot of money," {he} says. {He} offers you a hand.

choices.text: Say to put it on your account

effects.log: "I will," says {npc}, delighted, and {he} takes out a pencil. You will be seeing {him} again.

events.text: The whole teahouse goes quiet, and you look up from your bowl. It is {npc}. {He} has got older, and {he} has got fat, and {he} has got a very good knife. {He} takes the seat across from you, picks up your teapot, looks it over, and pours {him}self a cup without asking. "There was a sandbar," {he} says. "I have been thinking about it for quite a long time. Outside?"

choices.text: Say "outside"

effects.log: You finish your tea first, because you can. {npc} looks at you with approval. You go out together.

choices.text: Say that this time, only one of you is coming back in

effects.log: The other customers find they have somewhere to be. {npc} nods slowly and stands. {He} leaves {his} cup full, so that is what {he} thinks.

choices.text: Order another pot, and tell {him} your side of the sandbar

effects.log: You pay for it. By the end of the night you have both told the whole story twice, and each time you win. It is over.

choices.text: Leave {him} the teapot, and go home

effects.log: You go home. {npc} finishes your tea, smiling. You are both aware that this is not the end of it.

events.text: Your first teacher is a Bargemaster, {npc}, holding a very long pole and looks at you as if you were a shoal. "Everyone here is going to teach you something different," {he} says. "The Black Wind will teach you to hit. The Valley will teach you what not to eat. I will teach you the only thing that matters: what it costs. Every single thing. What did you do this morning, and what did it cost?"

choices.text: Add it all up for {him}, and borrow to learn more

effects.log: {npc} nods at each item. "You owe a bit less than you think," {he} says, "and I can lend you the rest of the lessons." You sign.

choices.text: Tell {him} what it cost someone else

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, and for the first time {he} looks as though someone has actually told {him} something. "Hm," {he} says. "That is the second lesson. Who told you?"

choices.text: Tell {him} you do not have to answer to a boatman

effects.log: The pole comes round very gently, and you are in the river. "That one is free," says {npc}.

events.text: {npc} has you all ashore to work a toll-gate for a week, with the Greenwood's young, on a road that does not belong to any of you. "Rule one," {he} says, "you may charge anyone anything. Rule two, you must still be able to use this road next year." A very old farmer is coming along with a cart of leeks and a look of great suffering, clearly having been through this a hundred times.

choices.text: Charge a fair toll, and borrow on the difference

effects.log: You let the cart through for a very small toll, and you are short at the end of the week. {npc} lends you the difference and writes it down, looking pleased. The farmer leaves a leek.

choices.text: Charge everything the farmer has got

effects.log: The farmer pays. It takes a long time to count out. {npc} says nothing. Next year, when you come back to this road, there are no carts at all.

choices.text: Wave the cart through, and pay the toll yourself

effects.log: {npc} looks at you sideways. "You will never be rich," {he} says, "but you might live." It costs you your supper.

events.text: A teacher from the Ten Thousand Poison Valley comes aboard for a month, with a basket. {npc}, who has known this teacher for forty years, stands well clear and calls the old poisoner the best there is. The School pays extra for the first lesson with eyes open. Everyone takes one mouthful of what is in the bowl. It costs extra, of course, for the antidote. There is a sliding scale, and {npc} holds the book.

choices.text: Take the mouthful, and buy the good antidote on credit

effects.log: You are very ill for an afternoon, and you learn eleven things. You also now owe {npc} rather a lot. {He} looks happy about both.

choices.text: Swap your bowl with the loudest boy on the barge

effects.log: The boy turns a very interesting colour. The Valley's teacher looks at you and smiles a very small smile. {npc} charges you for the antidote.

choices.text: Refuse the bowl, on principle

effects.log: The Valley's teacher shrugs. "Principles are also a poison, but they take longer." {npc} crosses something off.

events.text: Your last spring, {npc} takes you out in a small boat before dawn and hands you the book. It is everything you owe, in {his} own bad hand, and it is a good deal less than you had thought. "I have been fiddling it," {he} says. "Some people then swear something, a rule of their own, to have one thing nobody can buy off them. I always thought that was soft." {He} looks at the water. "I have got one myself."

choices.text: Swear yours, out here, on the water

effects.log: There is nobody to hear but {npc} and a heron. {npc} takes off {his} hat. You had no idea {he} was bald.

choices.text: Say you do not need favours, and add it back on

effects.log: {npc} looks at you and takes up the pole again. "Of course you do not," {he} says. {He} sounds proud, and very slightly disappointed.

choices.text: Say thank you

effects.log: It is possibly the first time anyone has said that on this river. {npc} goes red to the ears, and tells you to mind your own business, and to steer.

events.text: {npc} has run the third barge for thirty years, and this year the Water Gang wants to retire {him}. {He} tells you this while mending a net. {He} also tells you where {he} has hidden a very large sum of money, and goes on mending. It is either a test, or a joke, or the last lesson, or the only way {he} has of saying something. You have about a season to work out which.

choices.text: Add it to {his} account, and tell {him} where you moved it

effects.log: You move it somewhere better. {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. "Good," {he} says. "Now you may have some." You take a little, and write it down.

choices.text: Swear to look after it, and mean it

effects.log: You swear something, there by the nets, that has nothing to do with money, and you both know that. {He} goes on mending.

choices.text: Go and tell the Water Gang they are fools to retire {him}

effects.log: They laugh at you, and then, oddly, they do not retire {him}. {npc} will never admit to having heard about it. {He} gives you the good net.

events.text: The barges tie up for a day at the Autumn Landing, and for once nobody is teaching anybody anything. There is a fair. There are dumplings. {npc} has got hold of some silver, you do not ask how, and proposes that for one whole day you both act like people who have never heard of the Greenwood, and go and look at the man with the performing goose. {He} says the goose is a fraud. {He} is very serious.

choices.text: Go and expose the goose

effects.log: The goose bites {npc}. You laugh until you can hardly stand. The goose, you both agree, is not a fraud, and it is the finest thing either of you has ever seen.

choices.text: Spend the day checking the purser's figures

effects.log: You find an error in your favour. It is a very good day, in its way. {npc} comes back at night with one sleeve missing, and does not tell you about it.

events.text: It is the long slow reach, in the summer, and the barge has been going past the same reed beds for a week. Nothing is happening. There is nothing whatsoever to do. {npc} is lying on {his} back on the roof of the cabin with a straw in {his} mouth, and {he} has just asked you what you would do, if you did not owe anybody anything. {He} sounds as though {he} is really asking. It is very hot.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth

effects.log: You have never said it out loud before. {npc} does not laugh. {He} thinks about it for about a mile, and then tells you {his}. It is about a goat farm.

choices.text: Say you would buy up {his} debts

effects.log: {npc} laughs and puts the straw back. It is a good joke. It takes you a mile or so to notice neither of you has said anything else.

events.text: The fever comes up the river with the rain, and half the stern is flat on its back. {npc} is very bad. The purser comes by, looks down at {him}, and adds the cost of a doctor to the account, with a look you have not seen before. Nobody here owes {npc} anything at all. The doctor will come for the money, but the night is a long one, and somebody has got to keep {him} cool.

choices.text: Sit up with {him}, and put the doctor on your account

effects.log: {npc} never does find out how much you paid for it, or so {he} says. But years later {he} can tell you the exact amount.

choices.text: Leave it to those who are paid for it

effects.log: It is what anyone on the river would do. {npc} pulls through, and nods to you the next week, and {he} does not forget, and {he} does not hold it against you either. That is worse.

events.text: A big bearded person, {npc}, comes along the plank in boots that have never been wet, buys tea for the third barge, and watches you bail. {He} speaks for a Chief of the Seventy-Two, {he} says, or perhaps for all of them. {He} would be prepared, {he} says, to buy your whole debt off the School, as a kind of investment. You would just owe {him} instead. It is a very good rate.

choices.text: Shake on it

effects.log: {npc} has a very big hand. You now have somebody who will be furious if you die. It is surprisingly comforting.

choices.text: Say your debt is not for sale

effects.log: {npc} is very amused. "Everything is," {he} says, "but you go on and find that out." {He} tips the pole-boy, and walks back up the plank, and {his} boots are still dry.

events.text: There is someone sitting on the end of your bunk. You did not hear anyone come in. It is {npc}, who teaches knots on the fifth barge, and {he} says in a voice like a page turning that the Pavilion takes an interest in people who read the small print. {He} slides a thin piece of paper across the blanket. "Someone would speak for you," {he} says. "You would never know who. That is the service."

choices.text: Put your thumb on it

effects.log: You put your thumb on it, and when you look up, the paper is gone, and so is {npc}. You feel slightly safer, and you wonder who else has been in here.

choices.text: Push it back, and ask {him} to knock next time

effects.log: There is a very faint sound. It might be a laugh. In the morning, there is a neat new knot tied in your bootlace, and it takes you a week to undo.

events.text: Old {npc} is one of the Water Gang's own, and owns a slice of everything from here to the sea. {He} has noticed how you take a bend, and tells you, while gutting a fish, that a person might do worse than have a friend on the river. {He} does not want anything for it now. {He} mentions a landing or two that you might keep an eye on, later. {He} gives you the head of the fish, which you gather is an honour.

choices.text: Eat the fish head, and thank {him}

effects.log: It looks at you the whole time. {npc} watches you get through it, and {he} roars with laughter, and thumps your back. You have got a friend on the river, it seems.

choices.text: Say you will think about it, and hand back the head

effects.log: {npc} looks at it, and at you, and takes it back. "Think, then," {he} says. "The river does not, and it gets there."

events.text: Here she is, ring of keys and all, sitting on your wall and eating your plums. "Your account," says the purser, and opens the book. It has grown. It always does. {sda_cost} taels will close it. Or there is a small matter on the river that the School would like handled by someone who cannot be connected to the School. "{sda_teacher} sends regards. Well? I have got other plums."

choices.text: Pay it off: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You count it into her hand. She writes "Closed", and then, as she goes, she looks back. "You are the ninth, ever," she says. You keep the page.

choices.text: Handle the small matter

effects.log: She tells you where and when. You are, after all, very good at reading the small print. This time, you try not to.

choices.text: Tell her the account can stay open

effects.log: "It will," she says, cheerfully. She takes the last plum. A week later, she has sold your paper to somebody who is not at all cheerful.

events.text: A very small boy has brought you a very large bill. On the back of it someone has drawn a heron, which you recognise. The River School presents its compliments, along with four years of tuition, the doctor, the good rope, one goose, and interest, in all {sda_cost} taels. Alternatively, there is a boat that needs to go missing. The boy waits. He has clearly been told to wait, and is eating something.

choices.text: Pay the boy: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You pay him, and you give him something for himself. He looks at it with great suspicion, and bites it. You were just like him.

choices.text: See about the boat

effects.log: It goes missing. It is a neat bit of work. Someone, far away, is going to have a very bad year because of it.

choices.text: Dispute the goose

effects.log: You write them a very good letter about the goose. It is your best work. They send someone back to discuss it with you, in person, at length.

events.text: You are busy when the Water Gang's man walks in and sets a ledger down on the table in front of everyone. He does not raise his voice. The River School, he says, has sold on a number of its old accounts this year, and yours is one, and it can be closed today for {sda_cost} taels, or for a day's work with no questions. He looks around the room. "I can come back," he says, "with friends."

choices.text: Put the silver on the ledger: {sda_cost} taels

effects.log: You pay it, in front of everyone, without looking away from him. It is an expensive way to look good, and it is worth every tael.

choices.text: Give him the day's work

effects.log: It is a long day. It is the kind of day you learned on the third barge. You do not mention it to the people you were with.

choices.text: Tell him to bring his friends

effects.log: He nods, and takes the ledger back. "I will tell them you said so," he says. "They do like to be asked."

events.text: There is a very fat person at the next table, in very good boots, who is telling a roomful of strangers a long story about the time they stole a duck. It is a complete lie. You were there. It is {npc}. {He} sees you, stops in the middle of a word, and without any pause at all starts telling them about you, and it is an even bigger lie. Then {he} tells them you are paying.

choices.text: Pay, and tell them what really happened

effects.log: You tell it better. {He} corrects you, wrongly. You are thrown out together at dawn, and you are both in very good voice.

choices.text: Say you do not know this person, and leave

effects.log: {npc} stops, for just a moment. Then {he} goes straight on, a bit louder. The story has changed, you hear, by the time you get to the door.

events.text: A letter from {npc}. It has clearly been through several hands, and someone has charged for each. {He} has got that goat farm. {He} would like you to know that goats are dreadful, and the farm is doing badly, and {he} has never been so content, and that if you should ever need somewhere nobody would think to look for you, the goats do not talk. There is an invoice for the letter, enclosed.

choices.text: Pay the invoice, and send a very rude goat joke

effects.log: You write it out with great care. In due course, an invoice comes back for the laugh. You frame it.

choices.text: Keep the address, and send no answer

effects.log: You keep it somewhere safe. A person should always know where the back door is. You do not write. You will, you tell yourself, some other year.

events.text: You come out of a bad day into a worse evening, and {npc} is leaning on your gate. {He} says {he} heard you might be in some trouble. {He} has brought a rope, a bag of silver and a very thin knife, and {he} wants to know, with no great interest, which you would like. It has been a long time. {He} has not asked what you have been doing. It has never been the custom, on the river, to ask.

choices.text: Ask {him} to just come in and sit down

effects.log: {He} looks almost embarrassed. {He} leaves the rope on the step. You talk until very late, and it is mostly about the dry corner.

choices.text: Take the silver, and write {him} a receipt

effects.log: You write it, and sign it. {npc} checks it and folds it, with something that could be approval. It is a very good receipt.

events.text: {npc} has come up by boat with news and a piece of paper. There is, {he} says, some competition for the seat among the children. {He} and a couple of others from the old stern happen to hold a certain amount of paper on people who count. They could call it in, all on one day, in favour of whoever you say. It would not be cheap for the rest of them. {He} is mending something as {he} talks.

choices.text: Tell {him} to call it in for {sda_side}

effects.log: {npc} nods. "The safe way," {he} says. It does not sound like praise. The paper starts to move the next morning.

choices.text: Back the one nobody expects

effects.log: {npc} grins with all the teeth {he} still has. "Now that," {he} says, "is what we taught you." {He} is off before you can say anything else.

choices.text: Tell {him} the children are not a horse race

effects.log: "Everything is," says {npc}, but {he} tucks the paper away, and goes off to see about the tide. For now, {he} stays out.

events.text: There is a song going round the river now about the heirs, with a verse for each, and {npc} sings you the worst of it in a low voice. It is rather shocking how well they know the household. {He} and the old stern could lean on the singers, {he} says, in a friendly way, and when the river sings a name long enough, people on the shore start to believe it. {He} would hate to be wrong, so {he} thought {he} would ask.

choices.text: Give {him} {sda_side}'s name for the good verse

effects.log: It gets out, naturally. By the next new moon, {sda_side} has a good many new friends, all of them humming.

choices.text: Have them sing up the one nobody sings about

effects.log: {npc} goes very quiet, the way {he} did at the gorge. "You had better be right," {he} says, grinning. There is nothing to do then but make it so.

choices.text: Tell {him} to have them sing about you outliving them all

effects.log: That makes {him} laugh out loud. "Nobody would believe it," {he} says, and {he} never brings it up again.

events.text: They bring {sda_teacher} past you at the last, on a flat barge with a lamp in the bow. It is how it is done on the river. They do not stop. Somebody on board is calling out the account as they go, the whole long reckoning of what that old terror was owed, reach by reach. It goes on for a good while. You find you are on it. It takes you a moment to understand that you were one of the things {sda_teacher} was owed.

choices.text: Call out your own account across the water

effects.log: You shout it, all of it, what you owe. It is a great deal more than the book ever said. Someone on the barge writes it down, and marks it paid.

choices.text: Take off your hat, and do not say a word

effects.log: You stand there until the lamp goes round the bend. It costs nothing, and you have never in your life been so sure you have paid in full.
